risk-of-bias.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"The unit of randomization was the family, making it a cluster-randomized trial. We stratified the families by the children’s baseline plasma B12 concentrations; those below and above the median value were equally distributed in six groups. Within each group, the statistician randomly allocated codes (A–F) to the participant families."

"Table 1 shows the basic characteristics of the 300 participants. Seventy-two percent fathers, 48% mothers and 27% children were B12 deficient, and 75% fathers, 35% mothers and 47% children were hyperhomocysteinemic. In contrast, only 14% fathers, 8% mothers and 2% children had folate deficiency. Baseline B12, folate and tHcy concentrations were similar in the different supplementation groups."

"The participants were families from an ‘extended’ cohort of the PMNS. The PMNS methodology has been reported in detail by Rao et al. (2001)."

"Of these, 119 families remain in follow-up, and the child and parents (349 individuals) were invited to take part in this study."

Comment: 1a. Supplements were similar in appearance with contents known to pharmacist suggesting allocation concealment prior to assignment to clusters. Authors report the use of a random number generation method for randomisation of clusters. Baseline differences in biochemical markers between intervention groups are presented; however, authors report no socio-demographic characteristics at baseline by intervention clusters. Limited information to permit judgment on baseline comparability of clusters.

1b. Authors report a sub-sample of the PMNS cohort was recruited for this study (Figure 1). It is not explicitly stated whether all clusters (families) were identified and consented prior to randomisation. There is indication that families or individuals were recruited post-randomisation; however, the timeline is unclear. No evidence of baseline imbalances across clusters is reported in Table 1 that might suggest differential recruitment.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"Of the 119 families (349 individuals) in the extended PMNS cohort, 307 individuals were willing to participate (88% response), 7 (1 pregnant, 6 anemic) were excluded and 300 (106 children, 93 fathers and 101 mothers) were randomized (Figure 1). During the intervention, one woman became pregnant and five participants received B12-containing medication (from family physician) and were excluded from the analysis. Three participants withdrew and one was lost to follow-up after collection of the 4-month sample; they were analyzed using the Last Observation Carried Forward method. Thus, the final analysis includes 294 participants (106 children, 92 fathers and 96 mothers)."

Comment: It is likely that participants were unaware of the composition of supplements received and thus assigned intervention clusters. Trial investigators were blinded to supplement composition and allocated clusters which were revealed after data collection. 

The intervention was successful for 98% (294/300) of randomized participants. There is no clear indication that failures occurred in the implementation of the intervention. 

Reasons for loss to follow-up include: pregnancy, receipt of vitamin B12 supplements outside of the intervention, and withdrawal. Other reasons are not reported for withdrawal (n=3) and loss to follow-up (n=1); however, the proportions are small enough to have little to no effect on the outcome. It is not likely that non-adherence may have affected the outcome by cluster.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "Of the 119 families (349 individuals) in the extended PMNS cohort, 307 individuals were willing to participate (88% response), 7 (1 pregnant, 6 anemic) were excluded and 300 (106 children, 93 fathers and 101 mothers) were randomized (Figure 1). During the intervention, one woman became pregnant and five participants received B12-containing medication (from family physician) and were excluded from the analysis. Three participants withdrew and one was lost to follow-up after collection of the 4-month sample; they were analyzed using the Last Observation Carried Forward method. Thus, the final analysis includes 294 participants (106 children, 92 fathers and 96 mothers)."

"In brief, 119 families (parents and children trios) from the extended PMNS were randomized in groups and supplemented daily for 12 months with B12 (10 µg) and/or folic acid (200 µg), to investigate their effect on plasma homocysteine levels. We randomly selected 12 children (out of a total 15–17 children per group) from each of the four supplementation groups – placebo (B0F0), folic acid (B0F200), B12 (B10F0), B12 + folic acid acid (B10F200), and compared their methylome before and after supplementation (Figure 1)."

Comment: Authors report limited information on outcome data available for all eligible and randomised clusters (and specifically for children). Outcome data were available for 16% (48/300) of recruited, eligible and randomised participants within clusters. Authors report insufficient information on sensitivity analysis or other analysis methods to assess relationship between missingness of the outcome and its true value. Outcome data are reported for a sub-sample of randomised participants within clusters. Other reasons for missing outcomes include: protocol deviation, pregnancy, withdrawal and loss to follow-up. Reasons reported are unassociated with the true value of the outcome by cluster.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "Height was measured to the nearest 0.1cm using a wall mounted stadiometer (CMS Instruments, London, UK) and body weight to the nearest 0.005 kg (Conveigh, Electronic Instruments Ltd, Mumbai, India). Dietary intake of B12-and folate-rich foods was recorded by food frequency questionnaire in children at the beginning and end of 12 months."

"Detailed physical and biochemical measurements (B12, folate and homocysteine concentrations) and white blood cell counts at baseline and one-year follow-up were measured using standard techniques as described earlier [12]."

"The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

Comment: There is indication that anthropometric method conforms to a valid and appropriate method. Authors allude to standardised procedures suggesting the use of comparable methods across intervention clusters and time points. Insufficient information is provided to permit judgement of whether outcome assessors were aware of the conduct of the trial. Limited information is reported; however, only a third-party pharmacist was aware of supplement composition, suggesting that trial investigators and research personnel were likely blinded to intervention cluster allocations.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The present study included children from the Pune Maternal Nutrition Study (PMNS), which was established to examine the relationship between maternal nutrition status, fetal growth and long-term outcomes in the children [13]. The study design of the B12/ folic acid intervention in the extended PMNS cohort has been described earlier [12]."

"Height was measured to the nearest 0.1 cm using a wall mounted stadiometer (CMS Instruments, London, UK) and body weight to the nearest 0.005 kg (Conveigh, Electronic Instruments Ltd, Mumbai, India). Dietary intake of B12-and folate-rich foods was recorded by food frequency questionnaire in children at the beginning and end of 12 months."

"The data are presented as mean and standard deviation (s.d.). Though B12 and tHcy concentrations were not normally distributed, we used parametric tests for differences between group means, which are normally distributed as per the central limit theorem. We used analysis of variance to test the differences between supplementation groups, adjusting for the cluster design. There was no difference between clustered and unclustered analysis (statistically insignificant intraclass correlation)."

Comment: Recruitment for the trial was from 01/04/2007 to 31/03/2008. The trial was registered on 07/09/2007. From the trials registry (ISRCTN59289820), the outcome is pre-specified as a secondary outcome measure: "Body composition (anthropometry, Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry [DEXA])* -- to be measured only in children" Outcome reported is in accordance with timepoints and methods reported with no indication of selection from multiple outcome measurements.

Analysis of the outcome reported conforms to the pre-specified analysis plan. There is no clear indication that numerical results were selectively reported from multiple analyses on the basis of the results from allocated clusters.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote:  "Included children were randomized to 3 groups to receive one bar per day, fortified mg with (a) 2 B12 or (b) multiple micronutrients mg (MMN), including 1.82 B12 (United Nations 12 Children’s Emergency Fund guidelines (Supplementary Table 1), or (c) no added micronutrients (placebo). All bars were similar in appearance."

"Randomization was computer generated, and stratification was based on baseline B12 and hemoglobin concentrations (below and above median) to ensure comparable distribution."

"We approached 180 school children and their parents to participate in the trial, of whom 178 (99%) agreed. Fourteen children were excluded: 13 with B12 <100 pmol/L and 1 with anemia; they were prescribed appropriate treatment (Figure 1A). The 164 randomized children (57% girls) were 11.3 (10.9-12.0) years old, 139.4 (134.5-144.5) cm tall and with a weight of 28.8 (25.2-33.4) kg; there was no significant difference between groups. Plasma B12, folate, and homocysteine concentrations were comparable (Table 1)."

Comment: The method of allocation concealment were not reported; however, nutrient composition of nutrient bars were probably concealed prior to assignment. Authors report a sound method of random number generation. Authors report no differences in baseline characteristics between intervention groups.

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote:  "As part of our research to improve B12 status of the population, we tested 2 B12 fortified food items: (1) A nutrient bar in school children, and (2) Yogurt in adults, for their efficacy to improve B12 status."

"Significance of the differences between baseline and end of trial levels of clinical and biochemical measurements were tested by paired t-test for continuous variables and by test for categorical variables. Significance of difference from placebo group was tested by t-test.

"We used multivariate regression analysis to calculate predictors of change in B12 and homocysteine concentrations after intervention. We normalized the variables by converting them to standard deviation scores. We used age, sex, BMI, baseline concentrations of B12 or homocysteine, and dose of B12 and folic acid in intervention group as determinants of change."

Comment: Recruitment for the trial was from September 2011 to March 2012 with the trial registered on 16/07/2012. Based on the trials registry (CTRI/2012/07/002799), the outcome is pre-specified as follows: "Data (height, weight and venous blood sample) will be collected at baseline and after 5 months." Outcome measurement methods and results are reported in the published report according to a pre-specified analysis plan. Analysis of outcome results at baseline and post-intervention with differences within and between groups are reported as specified in the statistical analysis plan. Minimal indication of selection of outcome data on the basis of results from multiple analyses.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote:  "A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp). The intervention was a lipid-based nutritional supplement prepared by NUTRISET Ltd and was provided in jars prelabeled with the subject identification number. The placebo and the vitamin supplements were identical in appearance and taste. The treatment allocation was masked to the study participants and the study team throughout the data collection period."

"Using a factorial design, we randomly assigned eligible children to 1 of 4 treatment groups: 1) placebo (n = 249), 2) 2 times the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)4 of folic acid (n = 249), 3) 2 times the RDA of vitamin B-12 (n = 252), and 4) a combination of both vitamin B-12 and folic acid (n = 250) in blocks of 16. A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp)."

"The baseline features were similar in the 4 groups."

Comment: A third-party scientist was involved in random scheme generation and supplements were similar in appearance suggesting that the allocation sequence may have been concealed prior to assignment. Authors report a random number sequence generation method. Author report and visual inspection of Table 1 suggests no substantial differences in baseline characteristics between treatment groups. Any observable differences are compatible with chance findings.

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote:  "A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp). The intervention was a lipid-based nutritional supplement prepared by NUTRISET Ltd and was provided in jars prelabeled with the subject identification number. The placebo and the vitamin supplements were identical in appearance and taste. The treatment allocation was masked to the study participants and the study team throughout the data collection period."

Trials registry (NCT00717730): Masking: Quadruple (Participant, Care Provider, Investigator, Outcomes Assessor).

"Of the randomly assigned children, 99% were available for the last scheduled visit, ie, only 7 children withdrew."

"Compliance was good, and 96% of the scheduled doses were reportedly ingested. Compliance was reflected in the change in plasma concentrations of folate, vitamin B-12, and tHcy from baseline to the end of the study (Table 2). At the end of the study, the children who received vitamin B-12 supplements (± folic acid) had a geometric mean vitamin B-12 concentration that was 1.28 times (95% CI: 1.14, 1.44) that of children in the placebo and folic acid groups. Similarly, the geometric mean folate concentration was 3.14 (95% CI: 2.56, 3.86) higher among the folic acid recipients. Either vitamin B-12 or folic acid supplementation alone resulted in a decreased tHcy concentration, with geometric mean ratios of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.72, 0.83) and 0.83 (95% CI: 0.77, 0.89), respectively."

Comment: There is indication from the published report and trials registry that participants, investigators and carers delivering the intervention were blinded to treatment groups. Out of 1000 children (6-30 months) randomised, almost all (~99%; 993/1000) participants returned for the last trial visit suggesting the intervention was successful for most participants. Authors report increased ingestion of supplementation with observed changes in vitamin B12, folate and homocysteine concentrations, as expected between treatment groups. These observations suggest good adherence to study protocol and unlikely to impact reported outcome.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "Of 1377 eligible children aged 6 to 30 mo, we randomly assigned 1000 children into the study."

"The flow of the participants through the study is shown in Fig 1. Of the 1000 children in the main study, we established contact with 798 children, of whom 791 children consented to participate."

"The study enrolled children from January 2010 to September 2011. Neurodevelopment was added during the first phase as a secondary outcome. We were only able to include the last 422 children for these assessments (10). In September 2016, we attempted to approach all the children in the original trial. Of the 1000 children in the main study, we established contact with 798 children, of whom 791 children consented to participate in the study."

Comment: Outcome data were available and analysed for a sub-sample [~79%; n=791) of 1000 children (6-30 months) randomized. Outcome data were analysed in a sub-sample of participants with no analysis methods or sensitivity analysis to ascertain the relationship between the sub-selected outcome data (analysed vs. not re-enroled) and its true value. Authors report only analysing outcome data in a sub-selected sample of randomised children; thus, missingness in the outcome data are unrelated to the true value of the outcome.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fourth Edition (India) (WISC-IVINDIA) is an assessment tool of intellectual ability in children validated for the Indian population with Indian norms (16). We conducted 7 subtests that summed up to 3 index scores: Perceptual Reasoning, Processing Speed, and Working Memory (Table 1). We did not conduct tests included in the Verbal Comprehension Index because these tests require English-language skills (16)."

"The Crichton Vocabulary Scales (CVS) covers verbal skills in children 4 to 11 years (17). The CVS is translated to Hindi, with Indian norms providing score a standardized total (18) (Table 1)."

"We calculated a combined WISC-IVINDIA and CVS z score on the basis of converted z scores on each subtest and a combined NEPSY-II z score on the basis of converted z scores in 7 subtests."

"Five psychologists blinded to the intervention groups undertook all assessments after training and standardization in 20 children per tester. Ten percent of all assessments were scored by 2 psychologists, of whom 1 performed the assessments and the other observed and scored. From these double scorings, we attained a coefficient of >96%, indicating excellent interrater agreement."

Trials registry (NCT00717730): Masking: Quadruple (Participant, Care Provider, Investigator, Outcomes Assessor).

Comment: Method used in outcome assessment conforms to a valid and appropriate method for assessing cognitive function using a tool validated for this population. The use of a standardised method with quality control measures such as training, and high inter-rater reliability in outcome assessment ensures comparable methods across treatment groups and time points. Outcome assessors were unaware of treatment group assignments.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The study enrolled children from January 2010 to September 2011. Neurodevelopment was added during the first phase as a secondary outcome."

"Scores on the cognitive tests were calculated on the basis of available norms (Table 1). We calculated a combined WISC-IVINDIA and CVS z score on the basis of converted z scores on each subtest and a combined NEPSY-II z score on the basis of converted z scores in 7 subtests (Inhibition-Naming versus Inhibition Contrast Scaled Score, Design Fluency Total Scaled Score, Word Generation-Semantic versus Initial Letter Contrast Scaled Score, Visuomotor Precision Combined Scaled Score, Manual Motor Sequences Total Score [raw score], Affect Recognition Total Scaled Score, and Geometric Puzzles Total Scaled Score)."

"We present mean (SD) scores for the cognitive tests in the intervention groups. We compared the intervention groups with the placebo group in linear regression models, in which the intervention groups were included as dummy variables and compared against the placebo group."

Comment: Recruitment for the trial was from January 2010 to September 2011. Trial (NCT00717730) was registered on 2008-07-16. In trials registry (CTRI/2016/11/007494), it is defined as an outcome to be measured at enrollment (5-6 years after supplementation) but limited information is provided. While the outcome is not specified in the trials registry, there is indication from the published report that the outcome results reported at the 6 to 9 year follow-up period are consistent with a pre-specified analysis plan. Based on the statistical analysis plan, numerical results were reported accordingly as means (SD) at the 6 to 9 year follow-up for all treatment groups. There is no indication that outcome results are selected from multiple eligible analysis.

Quote: "The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"The unit of randomization was the family, making it a cluster-randomized trial. We stratified the families by the children’s baseline plasma B12 concentrations; those below and above the median value were equally distributed in six groups. Within each group, the statistician randomly allocated codes (A–F) to the participant families."

"Table 1 shows the basic characteristics of the 300 participants. Seventy-two percent fathers, 48% mothers and 27% children were B12 deficient, and 75% fathers, 35% mothers and 47% children were hyperhomocysteinemic. In contrast, only 14% fathers, 8% mothers and 2% children had folate deficiency. Baseline B12, folate and tHcy concentrations were similar in the different supplementation groups."

"The participants were families from an ‘extended’ cohort of the PMNS. The PMNS methodology has been reported in detail by Rao et al. (2001)."

"Of these, 119 families remain in follow-up, and the child and parents (349 individuals) were invited to take part in this study."

Comment: 1a. Supplements were similar in appearance with contents known to pharmacist suggesting allocation concealment prior to assignment to clusters. Authors report the use of a random number generation method for randomisation of clusters. Baseline differences in biochemical markers between intervention groups are presented; however, authors report no socio-demographic characteristics at baseline by intervention clusters. Limited information to permit judgment on baseline comparability of clusters.

1b. Authors report a sub-sample of the PMNS cohort was recruited for this study (Figure 1). It is not explicitly stated whether all clusters (families) were identified and consented prior to randomisation. There is indication that families or individuals were recruited post-randomisation; however, the timeline is unclear. No evidence of baseline imbalances across clusters is reported in Table 1 that might suggest differential recruitment.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The trial was double blinded. We planned to test three levels of B12 supplementation (none, 2 and 10 mg) and each of these at two levels of folic acid supplementation (none and 200 mg), forming six groups (A = B0F0, B = B2F0, C = B10F0, D = B0F200, E = B2F200 and F = B10F200) (Figure 1)."

"The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"Of the 119 families (349 individuals) in the extended PMNS cohort, 307 individuals were willing to participate (88% response), 7 (1 pregnant, 6 anemic) were excluded and 300 (106 children, 93 fathers and 101 mothers) were randomized (Figure 1). During the intervention, one woman became pregnant and five participants received B12-containing medication (from family physician) and were excluded from the analysis. Three participants withdrew and one was lost to follow-up after collection of the 4-month sample; they were analyzed using the Last Observation Carried Forward method. Thus, the final analysis includes 294 participants (106 children, 92 fathers and 96 mothers)."

Comment: This was a double-blind cluster randomised trial with participants unaware of the composition of supplements received and thus, assigned intervention clusters.

Trial investigators were blinded to supplement composition and allocated clusters which were revealed after data collection.

The intervention was successful for 98% (294/300) of randomized participants. There is no clear indication that failures occurred in the implementation of the intervention.

Reasons for loss to follow-up include: pregnancy, receipt of vitamin B12 supplements outside of the intervention, and withdrawal. Other reasons are not reported for withdrawal (n=3) and loss to follow-up (n=1); however, the proportions are small enough to have little to no effect on the outcome. It is not likely that non-adherence may have affected the outcome by cluster.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "Of the 119 families (349 individuals) in the extended PMNS cohort, 307 individuals were willing to participate (88% response), 7 (1 pregnant, 6 anemic) were excluded and 300 (106 children, 93 fathers and 101 mothers) were randomized (Figure 1). During the intervention, one woman became pregnant and five participants received B12-containing medication (from family physician) and were excluded from the analysis. Three participants withdrew and one was lost to follow-up after collection of the 4-month sample; they were analyzed using the Last Observation Carried Forward method. Thus, the final analysis includes 294 participants (106 children, 92 fathers and 96 mothers)." "In brief, 119 families (parents and children trios) from the extended PMNS were randomized in groups and supplemented daily for 12 months with B12 (10 µg) and/or folic acid (200 µg), to investigate their effect on plasma homocysteine levels. We randomly selected 12 children (out of a total 15–17 children per group) from each of the four supplementation groups – placebo (B0F0), folic acid (B0F200), B12 (B10F0), B12 + folic acid acid (B10F200), and compared their methylome before and after supplementation (Figure 1)."

Comment: Authors report limited information on outcome data available for all eligible and randomized clusters (and specifically for children). 

Outcome data were available for 16% (48/300) of recruited, eligible and randomized participants within clusters.

Authors report insufficient information on sensitivity analysis or other analysis methods to assess relationship between missingness of the outcome and its true value.

Outcome data are reported for a sub-sample of randomized participants within clusters. Other reasons for missing outcomes include: protocol deviation, pregnancy, withdrawal and loss to follow-up. Reasons reported are unassociated with the true value of the outcome by cluster.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "Detailed physical and biochemical measurements (B12, folate and homocysteine concentrations) and white blood cell counts at baseline and one-year follow-up were measured using standard techniques as described earlier [12]."

"Digit span test: This test is a measure for working memory and is taken from Malin’s Intelligence Scale for Children. It consists of two parts, forward and backward. The longest digit string recalled is considered as the span [Personal communication]." 

"The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

Comment: From author request for unpublished data and study information, there is indication of the use of standardized procedures pertaining to physical assessments including cognitive tests as alluded to by authors. Limited information is reported on blinding of outcome assessors; however, only a third-party pharmacist was aware of supplement composition, suggesting that trial investigators and research personnel were likely blinded to intervention cluster allocations.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The present study included children from the Pune Maternal Nutrition Study (PMNS), which was established to examine the relationship between maternal nutrition status, fetal growth and long-term outcomes in the children [13]. The study design of the B12/ folic acid intervention in the extended PMNS cohort has been described earlier [12]."

"Detailed physical and biochemical measurements (B12, folate and homocysteine concentrations) and white blood cell counts at baseline and one-year follow-up were measured using standard techniques as described earlier [12]."

"The data are presented as mean and standard deviation (s.d.). Though B12 and tHcy concentrations were not normally distributed, we used parametric tests for differences between group means, which are normally distributed as per the central limit theorem. We used analysis of variance to test the differences between supplementation groups, adjusting for the cluster design. There was no difference between clustered and unclustered analysis (statistically insignificant intraclass correlation)."

Comment: Recruitment for the trial was from 01/04/2007 to 31/03/2008. The trial was registered on 07/09/2007. From the trials registry (ISRCTN59289820), the outcome is pre-specified as a secondary outcome measure: "Neuro-cognitive performance* -- to be measured only in children" Outcome reported is in accordance with timepoints and methods reported for other outcomes; no indication of selection from multiple outcome measurements.

Analysis of the outcome reported conforms to the pre-specified analysis plan. There is no clear indication that numerical results were selectively reported from multiple analyses on the basis of the results from allocated clusters.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote:  "A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp). The intervention was a lipid-based nutritional supplement prepared by NUTRISET Ltd and was provided in jars prelabeled with the subject identification number. The placebo and the vitamin supplements were identical in appearance and taste. The treatment allocation was masked to the study participants and the study team throughout the data collection period."

"Using a factorial design, we randomly assigned eligible children to 1 of 4 treatment groups: 1) placebo (n = 249), 2) 2 times the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)4 of folic acid (n = 249), 3) 2 times the RDA of vitamin B-12 (n = 252), and 4) a combination of both vitamin B-12 and folic acid (n = 250) in blocks of 16. A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp)."

"The baseline features were similar in the 4 groups."

Comment: A third-party scientist was involved in random scheme generation and supplements were similar in appearance suggesting that the allocation sequence may have been concealed prior to assignment. Authors report a random number sequence generation method. Author report and visual inspection of Table 1 suggests no substantial differences in baseline characteristics between treatment groups. Any observable differences are compatible with chance findings.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp). The intervention was a lipid based nutritional supplement prepared by NUTRISET Ltd and was provided in jars prelabeled with the subject identification number. The placebo and the vitamin supplements were identical in appearance and taste. The treatment allocation was masked to the study participants and the study team throughout the data collection period."

Trials registry (NCT00717730): Masking: Quadruple (Participant, Care Provider, Investigator, Outcomes Assessor).

"Of the randomly assigned children, 99% were available for the last scheduled visit, ie, only 7 children withdrew."

"Compliance was good, and 96% of the scheduled doses were reportedly ingested. Compliance was reflected in the change in plasma concentrations of folate, vitamin B-12, and tHcy from baseline to the end of the study (Table 2). At the end of the study, the children who received vitamin B-12 supplements (±folic acid) had a geometric mean vitamin B-12 concentration that was 1.28 times (95% CI: 1.14, 1.44) that of children in the placebo and folic acid groups. Similarly, the geometric mean folate concentration was 3.14 (95% CI: 2.56, 3.86) higher among the folic acid recipients. Either vitamin B-12 or folic acid supplementation alone resulted in a decreased tHcy concentration, with geometric mean ratios of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.72, 0.83) and 0.83 (95% CI: 0.77, 0.89), respectively."

Comment: There is indication from the published report and trials registry that participants, investigators and carers delivering the intervention were blinded to treatment groups. Out of 1000 children 6-30 months randomised, almost all (~99%; 993/1000) participants returned for the last trial visit suggesting the intervention was successful for most participants. Authors report increased ingestion of supplementation with observed changes in vitamin B12, folate and homocysteine concentrations as expected between treatment groups. These observations suggest good adherence to study protocol and unlikely to impact reported outcome.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "Of 1377 eligible children aged 6 to 30 mo, we randomly assigned 1000 children into the study."

"The flow of the participants through the study is shown in Fig 1. Of the 1000 children in the main study, we established contact with 798 children, of whom 791 children consented to participate."

"The study enrolled children from January 2010 to September 2011. Neurodevelopment was added during the first phase as a secondary outcome. We were only able to include the last 422 children for these assessments (10). In September 2016, we attempted to approach all the children in the original trial. Of the 1000 children in the main study, we established contact with 798 children, of whom 791 children consented to participate in the study."

Comment: Outcome data were available and analysed for a sub-sample [~79%; n=791) of 1000 children 6-30 months randomised. Outcome data were analyzed in a sub-sample of participants with no analysis methods or sensitivity analysis to ascertain the relationship between the sub-selected outcome data (analysed vs. not re-enroled) and its true value. Authors report only analysing outcome data in a sub-selected sample of randomized children; thus, missingness in the outcome data are unrelated to the true value of the outcome.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fourth Edition (India) (WISC-IVINDIA) is an assessment tool of intellectual ability in children validated for the Indian population with Indian norms (16). We conducted 7 subtests that summed up to 3 index scores: Perceptual Reasoning, Processing Speed, and Working Memory (Table 1). We did not conduct tests included in the Verbal Comprehension Index because these tests require English-language skills (16)."

"The Crichton Vocabulary Scales (CVS) covers verbal skills in children 4 to 11 years (17). The CVS is translated to Hindi, with Indian norms providing score a standardized total (18) (Table 1)."

"We calculated a combined WISC-IVINDIA and CVS z score on the basis of converted z scores on each subtest and a combined NEPSY-II z score on the basis of converted z scores in 7 subtests."

"Five psychologists blinded to the intervention groups undertook all assessments after training and standardization in 20 children per tester. Ten percent of all assessments were scored by 2 psychologists, of whom 1 performed the assessments and the other observed and scored. From these double scorings, we attained a coefficient of >96%, indicating excellent interrater agreement."

Trials registry (NCT00717730): Masking: Quadruple (Participant, Care Provider, Investigator, Outcomes Assessor).

Comment: Method used in outcome assessment conforms to a valid and appropriate method for assessing cognitive function using a tool validated for this population. The use of a standardized method with quality control measures such as training, and high inter-rater reliability in outcome assessment ensures comparable methods across treatment groups and time points. Outcome assessors were unaware of treatment group assignments.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The study enrolled children from January 2010 to September 2011. Neurodevelopment was added during the first phase as a secondary outcome."

"The Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fourth Edition (India)-IVINDIA) (WISC
is an assessment tool of intellectual ability in children validated for the Indian population .16 with Indian norms We conducted 7 subtests that summed up to 3 index
scores: Perceptual Reasoning, Processing Speed, and Working Memory (Table 1). We did not conduct tests included in the Verbal Comprehension Index because these
tests require English-language 16 skills."

"We present mean (SD) scores for the cognitive tests in the intervention groups. We compared the intervention groups with the placebo group in linear regression models, in which the intervention groups were included as dummy variables and compared against the placebo group."

Comment: Recruitment for the trial was from January 2010 to September 2011. Trial (NCT00717730) was registered on 2008-07-16. In trials registry (CTRI/2016/11/007494), it is defined as an outcome to be measured at enrollment (5-6 years after supplementation) but limited information is provided. While the outcome is not specified in the trials registry, there is indication from the published report that the outcome results reported at the 6 to 9 year follow-up period are consistent with a pre-specified analysis plan. Based on the statistical analysis plan, numerical results were reported accordingly as mean (SD) at the 6 to 9 year follow-up for all treatment groups. There is no indication that outcome results are selected from multiple eligible analysis.

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"The unit of randomization was the family, making it a cluster-randomized trial. We stratified the families by the children’s baseline plasma B12 concentrations; those below and above the median value were equally distributed in six groups. Within each group, the statistician randomly allocated codes (A–F) to the participant families."

"Table 1 shows the basic characteristics of the 300 participants. Seventy-two percent fathers, 48% mothers and 27% children were B12 deficient, and 75% fathers, 35% mothers and 47% children were hyperhomocysteinemic. In contrast, only 14% fathers, 8% mothers and 2% children had folate deficiency. Baseline B12, folate and tHcy concentrations were similar in the different supplementation groups."

"The participants were families from an ‘extended’ cohort of the PMNS. The PMNS methodology has been reported in detail by Rao et al. (2001)."

"Of these, 119 families remain in follow-up, and the child and parents (349 individuals) were invited to take part in this study."

Comment: 1a. Supplements were similar in appearance with contents known to pharmacist suggesting allocation concealment prior to assignment to clusters. Authors report the use of a random number generation method for randomisation of clusters. Baseline differences in biochemical markers between intervention groups are presented; however, authors report no socio-demographic characteristics at baseline by intervention clusters. Limited information to permit judgment on baseline comparability of clusters.

1b. Authors report a sub-sample of the PMNS cohort was recruited for this study (Figure 1). It is not explicitly stated whether all clusters (families) were identified and consented prior to randomisation. There is indication that families or individuals were recruited post-randomisation; however, the timeline is unclear. No evidence of baseline imbalances across clusters is reported in Table 1 that might suggest differential recruitment.

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:

"Of the 119 families (349 individuals) in the extended PMNS cohort, 307 individuals were willing to participate (88% response), 7 (1 pregnant, 6 anemic) were excluded and 300 (106 children, 93 fathers and 101 mothers) were randomised (Figure 1). During the intervention, one woman became pregnant and five participants received B12-containing medication (from family physician) and were excluded from the analysis. Three participants withdrew and one was lost to follow-up after collection of the 4-month sample; they were analyzed using the Last Observation Carried Forward method. Thus, the final analysis includes 294 participants (106 children, 92 fathers and 96 mothers)."

Comment: It is likely that participants were unaware of the composition of supplements received and thus assigned intervention clusters.

Trial investigators were blinded to supplement composition and allocated clusters which were revealed after data collection.

The intervention was successful for 98% (294/300) of randomised participants within clusters. There is no clear indication that failures occurred in the implementation of the intervention.

Reasons for loss to follow-up include: pregnancy, receipt of vitamin B12 supplements outside of the intervention, and withdrawal. Other reasons are not reported for withdrawal (n=3) and loss to follow-up (n=1); however, the proportions are small enough to have little to no effect on the outcome. It is not likely that non-adherence may have affected the outcome by cluster.

"Using a factorial design, we randomly assigned eligible children to 1 of 4 treatment groups: 1) placebo (n = 249), 2) 2 times the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)4 of folic acid (n = 249), 3) 2 times the RDA of vitamin B-12 (n = 252), and 4) a combination of both vitamin B-12 and folic acid (n = 250) in blocks of 16. risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"The unit of randomization was the family, making it a cluster-randomized trial. We stratified the families by the children’s baseline plasma B12 concentrations; those below and above the median value were equally distributed in six groups. Within each group, the statistician randomly allocated codes (A–F) to the participant families."

"Table 1 shows the basic characteristics of the 300 participants. Seventy-two percent fathers, 48% mothers and 27% children were B12 deficient, and 75% fathers, 35% mothers and 47% children were hyperhomocysteinemic. In contrast, only 14% fathers, 8% mothers and 2% children had folate deficiency. Baseline B12, folate and tHcy concentrations were similar in the different supplementation groups."

"The participants were families from an ‘extended’ cohort of the PMNS. The PMNS methodology has been reported in detail by Rao et al. (2001)."

"Of these, 119 families remain in follow-up, and the child and parents (349 individuals) were invited to take part in this study."

Comment: 1a. Supplements were similar in appearance with contents known to pharmacist suggesting allocation concealment prior to assignment to clusters. Authors report the use of a random number generation method for randomisation of clusters. Baseline differences in biochemical markers between intervention groups are presented; however, authors report no socio-demographic characteristics at baseline by intervention clusters. Limited information to permit judgment on baseline comparability of clusters.

1b. Authors report a sub-sample of the PMNS cohort was recruited for this study (Figure 1). It is not explicitly stated whether all clusters (families) were identified and consented prior to randomisation. There is indication that families or individuals were recruited post-randomisation; however, the timeline is unclear. No evidence of baseline imbalances across clusters is reported in Table 1 that might suggest differential recruitment.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"Of the 119 families (349 individuals) in the extended PMNS cohort, 307 individuals were willing to participate (88% response), 7 (1 pregnant, 6 anemic) were excluded and 300 (106 children, 93 fathers and 101 mothers) were randomized (Figure 1). During the intervention, one woman became pregnant and five participants received B12-containing medication (from family physician) and were excluded from the analysis. Three participants withdrew and one was lost to follow-up after collection of the 4-month sample; they were analyzed using the Last Observation Carried Forward method. Thus, the final analysis includes 294 participants (106 children, 92 fathers and 96 mothers)."

Comment: It is likely that participants were unaware of the composition of supplements received and thus assigned intervention clusters.

Trial investigators were blinded to supplement composition and allocated groups which were revealed after data collection.

The intervention was successful for 98% (294/300) of randomised participants. There is no clear indication that failures occurred in the implementation of the intervention.

Reasons for loss to follow-up include: pregnancy, receipt of vitamin B12 supplements outside of the intervention, and withdrawal. Other reasons are not reported for withdrawal (n=3) and loss to follow-up (n=1); however, the proportions are small enough to have little to no effect on the outcome. It is not likely that non-adherence may have affected the outcome by cluster.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "Blood samples were collected at baseline and 4 and 12 months after supplementation and were measured in separate batches. The samples were collected in EDTA tubes, kept on ice and spun within 1 h (2500 g 15 min) and plasma aliquots were stored (-70o C) until further analysis. Hemoglobin was measured within 1 h of blood collection on a Beckman Coulter Analyzer (AC.T diff; Miami, Florida). Plasma creatinine was measured on an Alcyon 300 automated analyzer (Abbott Laboratories, Abbott Park, IL, USA) using Jaffe’s method. Plasma B12 and folate were measured by microbiological assay using a colistin sulfate-resistant strain of Lactobacillus leichmannii (Kelleher et al., 1987; Kelleher and Broin, 1991) and a chloramphenicol-resistant strain of Lactobacillus casei (Horne and Patterson, 1988; Tamura et al., 1990) with inter-batch CV <8% and <7%, respectively.

"The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

Comment: Laboratory method conforms to an appropriate and valid method. Vitamin B12 deficiency was defined as vitamin B12 concentration less than 148 pmol/L.

The use of a standardised laboratory method suggests the use of comparable methods across intervention clusters and time points.

Insufficient information is provided to permit judgment of whether outcome assessors were aware of the conduct of the trial.

Limited information is reported; however, only a third-party pharmacist was aware of supplement composition, suggesting that trial investigators and research personnel were likely blinded to intervention cluster allocations.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The purpose of this paper was to study the effect of physiological doses of B12 and folic acid on plasma total homocysteine (tHcy) concentration." 

"Blood samples were collected at baseline and 4 and 12 months after supplementation and were measured in separate batches. The samples were collected in EDTA tubes, kept on ice and spun within 1 h (2500 g15 min) and plasma aliquots were stored (-70o C) until further analysis. Hemoglobin was measured within 1 h of blood collection on a Beckman Coulter Analyzer (AC.T diff; Miami, Florida). Plasma creatinine was measured on an Alcyon 300 automated analyzer (Abbott Laboratories, Abbott Park, IL, USA) using Jaffe’s method. Plasma B12 and folate were measured by microbiological assay using a colistin sulfate-resistant strain of Lactobacillus leichmannii (Kelleher et al., 1987; Kelleher and Broin, 1991) and a chloramphenicol-resistant strain of Lactobacillus casei (Horne and Patterson, 1988; Tamura et al., 1990) with inter-batch CV <8% and <7%, respectively."

"The data are presented as mean and standard deviation (s.d.). Though B12 and tHcy concentrations were not normally distributed, we used parametric tests for differences between group means, which are normally distributed as per the central limit theorem. We used analysis of variance to test the differences between supplementation groups, adjusting for the cluster design. There was no difference between clustered and unclustered analysis (statistically insignificant intraclass correlation)."

Comment: Recruitment for the trial was from 01/04/2007 to 31/03/2008. The trial was registered on 07/09/2007. From the trials registry (ISRCTN59289820), the outcome is pre-specified as a primary outcome measure: "Serum levels of vitamin B12, folate, tHcy, and MMA, measured at the end of four months and twelve months of supplementation." Outcome is reported are in accordance with timepoints and methods reported with no indication of selection from multiple outcome measurements.

Analysis of the outcome reported conforms to the pre-specified analysis plan. There is no clear indication that numerical results were selectively reported from multiple analyses on the basis of the results from allocated clusters.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote:  "A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp). The intervention was a lipid-based nutritional supplement prepared by NUTRISET Ltd and was provided in jars prelabeled with the subject identification number. The placebo and the vitamin supplements were identical in appearance and taste. The treatment allocation was masked to the study participants and the study team throughout the data collection period."

"Using a factorial design, we randomly assigned eligible children to 1 of 4 treatment groups: 1) placebo (n = 249), 2) 2 times the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)4 of folic acid (n = 249), 3) 2 times the RDA of vitamin B-12 (n = 252), and 4) a combination of both vitamin B-12 and folic acid (n = 250) in blocks of 16. A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp)."

"The baseline features were similar in the 4 groups."

Comment: A third-party scientist was involved in random scheme generation and supplements were similar in appearance suggesting that the allocation sequence may have been concealed prior to assignment. Authors report a random number sequence generation method. Author report and visual inspection of Table 1 suggests no substantial differences in baseline characteristics between treatment groups. Any observable differences are compatible with chance findings.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp). The intervention was a lipid based nutritional supplement prepared by NUTRISET Ltd and was provided in jars prelabeled with the subject identification number. The placebo and the vitamin supplements were identical in appearance and taste. The treatment allocation was masked to the study participants and the study team throughout the data collection period."

"Of the randomly assigned children, 99% were available for the last scheduled visit, ie, only 7 children withdrew."

"Compliance was good, and 96% of the scheduled doses were reportedly ingested. Compliance was reflected in the change in plasma concentrations of folate, vitamin B-12, and tHcy from baseline to the end of the study (Table 2). At the end of the study, the children who received vitamin B-12 supplements (± folic acid) had a geometric mean vitamin B-12 concentration that was 1.28 times (95% CI: 1.14, 1.44) that of children in the placebo and folic acid groups. Similarly, the geometric mean folate concentration was 3.14 (95% CI: 2.56, 3.86) higher among the folic acid recipients. Either vitamin B-12 or folic acid supplementation alone resulted in a decreased tHcy concentration, with geometric mean ratios of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.72, 0.83) and 0.83 (95% CI: 0.77, 0.89), respectively."

Comment: The trial registration states that masking was quadruple (participant, care provider, investigator and outcome assesor). There is indication from the published report and trials registry that participants were blinded to treatment groups.

Out of 1000 children 6-30 months randomised, almost all (993/1000) participants returned for the last trial visit suggesting the intervention was successful for most participants.

Authors report high ingestion of supplementation with observed changes in vitamin B12, folate and homocysteine concentrations as expected between treatment groups. These observations suggest good adherence to study protocol and unlikely to impact reported outcome.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The strength of our study was that it was a well-conducted randomized, placebo-controlled trial with very few losses to follow-up. Furthermore, compliance was excellent, as reflected by expected changes in plasma concentrations of vitamin B-12, folate, and tHcy at the end of the study."

"Of 1377 eligible children aged 6230 mo, we randomly assigned 1000 children into the study."

"Blood samples were obtained at baseline from all children and at end of the 26-wk supplementation period in a subsample of 16 randomly selected blocks (256 children); 3 mL blood was collected into an evacuated tube containing EDTA (Becton Dickinson)."

Comment: Authors mentioned that 99% of the randomised children were available for last visit and compliance was high; however, results at the end of study are only reported for about 30% of the participants in each group (Table 2).

Outcome data were analysed and available for a sub-sample (n=256) of 1000 children 6-30 months randomised.

Outcome data were analyzed in a sub-sample of participants with no analysis methods or sensitivity analysis to ascertain the relationship between the sub-selected outcome data (analyzed vs. not re-enrolled) and its true value. 

Authors report only analysing outcome data in a sub-selected sample of randomised children; thus, missingness in the outcome data are unrelated to the outcome.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The plasma was centrifuged at ~450 x g at room temperature for 10 min, separated, and transferred into storage vials and stored at 2200C until analyzed. Total homocysteine (tHcy) was analyzed by using commercial kits from Abbott Laboratories (18). Plasma concentrations of vitamin B-12 and folate were measured by using microbiological assays with a chloramphenicol-resistant strain of Lactobacillus casei and a colistin sulfate–resistant strain of Lactobacillus leichmannii, respectively (19)."

Comment: Laboratory method used in outcome assessment conforms to a valid and appropriate method. Vitamin B12 concentrations were discretely reported, with concentration < 150pmol/L being the indicator for vitamin B12 deficiency. 

No information is provided. However, the use of a standardised laboratory method in outcome assessment ensures comparable methods across treatment groups and time points.

Trials registry (NCT00717730): Masking: Quadruple (Participant, Care Provider, Investigator, Outcomes Assessor). In clinical trials registration, masking was quadruple (participant, care provider, investigator and outcome assesor). There is indication from the trials registry that outcome assessors were unaware of treatment group assignments.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The plasma was centrifuged at ~450 x g at room temperature for 10 min, separated, and transferred into storage vials and stored at 2208C until analyzed. Plasma concentrations of vitamin B-12 and folate were measured by using microbiological assays with a chloramphenicol-resistant strain of Lactobacillus casei and a colistin sulfate–resistant strain of Lactobacillus leichmannii, respectively (19)."

"One-third of the children had a vitamin B-12 concentration ≤200 pmol/L and almost one-third had a baseline folate concentration, 7.5 nmol/L. Elevated tHcy was seen in >50% of the children (Table 2)."

"At the end of the study, the children who received vitamin B-12 supplements (± folic acid) had a geometric mean vitamin B-12 concentration that was 1.28 times (95% CI: 1.14, 1.44) that of children in the placebo±folic acid groups."

"In the table of baseline data, continuous variables were reported as means or medians as appropriate and categorical variables as proportions. We log transformed the plasma folate, vitamin B-12, and tHcy concentrations. The mean differences and the corresponding 95% CIs were compared by using t- tests, and differences between the groups are expressed as geometric mean ratios."

Comment: Recruitment for the trial was from January 2010 to September 2011. Trial (NCT00717730) was registered on 2008-07-16. The outcome is pre-specified in the trials registry as: "Changes in folate, vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, and homocysteine concentration" with a timeframe of 6 months.

Based on the statistical analysis plan, numerical results were reported accordingly as medians at baseline and at the end of the study for all treatment groups. There is no indication that outcome results are selected from multiple eligible analysis.

Quote: "The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"The unit of randomization was the family, making it a cluster-randomized trial. We stratified the families by the children’s baseline plasma B12 concentrations; those below and above the median value were equally distributed in six groups. Within each group, the statistician randomly allocated codes (A–F) to the participant families."

"Table 1 shows the basic characteristics of the 300 participants. Seventy-two percent fathers, 48% mothers and 27% children were B12 deficient, and 75% fathers, 35% mothers and 47% children were hyperhomocysteinemic. In contrast, only 14% fathers, 8% mothers and 2% children had folate deficiency. Baseline B12, folate and tHcy concentrations were similar in the different supplementation groups."

"The participants were families from an ‘extended’ cohort of the PMNS. The PMNS methodology has been reported in detail by Rao et al. (2001)."

"Of these, 119 families remain in follow-up, and the child and parents (349 individuals) were invited to take part in this study."

Comment: 1a. Supplements were similar in appearance with contents known to pharmacist suggesting allocation concealment prior to assignment to clusters. Authors report the use of a random number generation method for randomisation of clusters. Baseline differences in biochemical markers between intervention groups are presented; however, authors report no socio-demographic characteristics at baseline by intervention clusters. Limited information to permit judgment on baseline comparability of clusters.

1b. Authors report a sub-sample of the PMNS cohort was recruited for this study (Figure 1). It is not explicitly stated whether all clusters (families) were identified and consented prior to randomisation. There is indication that families or individuals were recruited post-randomisation; however, the timeline is unclear. No evidence of baseline imbalances across clusters is reported in Table 1 that might suggest differential recruitment.

"Of the 119 families (349 individuals) in the extended PMNS cohort, 307 individuals were willing to participate (88% response), 7 (1 pregnant, 6 anemic) were excluded and 300 (106 children, 93 fathers and 101 mothers) were randomized (Figure 1). Three participants withdrew and one was lost to follow-up after collection of the 4-month sample; they were analyzed using the Last Observation Carried Forward method. Thus, the final analysis includes 294 participants (106 children, 92 fathers and 96 mothers)."

Comment: It is likely that participants were unaware of the composition of supplements received and thus assigned intervention clusters.

Trial investigators were blinded to supplement composition and allocated groups which were revealed after data collection.

Other reasons are not reported for withdrawal (n=3) and loss to follow-up (n=1); however, the proportions are small enough to have little to no effect on the outcome. All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"The unit of randomization was the family, making it a cluster-randomized trial. We stratified the families by the children’s baseline plasma B12 concentrations; those below and above the median value were equally distributed in six groups. Within each group, the statistician randomly allocated codes (A–F) to the participant families."

"Table 1 shows the basic characteristics of the 300 participants. Seventy-two percent fathers, 48% mothers and 27% children were B12 deficient, and 75% fathers, 35% mothers and 47% children were hyperhomocysteinemic. In contrast, only 14% fathers, 8% mothers and 2% children had folate deficiency. Baseline B12, folate and tHcy concentrations were similar in the different supplementation groups."

"The participants were families from an ‘extended’ cohort of the PMNS. The PMNS methodology has been reported in detail by Rao et al. (2001)."

"Of these, 119 families remain in follow-up, and the child and parents (349 individuals) were invited to take part in this study."

Comment: 1a. Supplements were similar in appearance with contents known to pharmacist suggesting allocation concealment prior to assignment to clusters. Authors report the use of a random number generation method for randomisation of clusters. Baseline differences in biochemical markers between intervention groups are presented; however, authors report no socio-demographic characteristics at baseline by intervention clusters. Limited information to permit judgment on baseline comparability of clusters.

1b. Authors report a sub-sample of the PMNS cohort was recruited for this study (Figure 1). It is not explicitly stated whether all clusters (families) were identified and consented prior to randomisation. There is indication that families or individuals were recruited post-randomisation; however, the timeline is unclear. No evidence of baseline imbalances across clusters is reported in Table 1 that might suggest differential recruitment.

"Compliance was good, and 96% of the scheduled doses were reportedly ingested. Compliance was reflected in the change in plasma concentrations of folate, vitamin B-12, and tHcy from baseline to the end of the study (Table 2). At the end of the study, the children who received vitamin B-12 supplements ( and folic acid) had a geometric mean vitamin B-12 concentration that was 1.28 times (95% CI: 1.14, 1.44) that of children in the placebo and folic acid groups. Similarly, the geometric mean folate concentration was 3.14 (95% CI: 2.56, 3.86) higher among the folic acid recipients. Comment: In clinical trials registration, masking was quadruple (participant, care provider, investigator and outcome assesor). There is indication from the published report and trials registry that participants and trial investigators were blinded to treatment groups. 

Out of 1000 children 6-30 months randomised, almost all (993/1000) participants returned for the last trial visit suggesting the intervention was successful for most participants. These observations suggest good adherence to study protocol and unlikely to impact reported outcome.

"Using a factorial design, we randomly assigned eligible children to 1 of 4 treatment groups: 1) placebo (n = 249), 2) 2 times the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)4 of folic acid (n = 249), 3) 2 times the RDA of vitamin B-12 (n = 252), and 4) a combination of both vitamin B-12 and folic acid (n = 250) in blocks of 16. risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"The unit of randomization was the family, making it a cluster-randomized trial. We stratified the families by the children’s baseline plasma B12 concentrations; those below and above the median value were equally distributed in six groups. Within each group, the statistician randomly allocated codes (A–F) to the participant families."

"Table 1 shows the basic characteristics of the 300 participants. Seventy-two percent fathers, 48% mothers and 27% children were B12 deficient, and 75% fathers, 35% mothers and 47% children were hyperhomocysteinemic. In contrast, only 14% fathers, 8% mothers and 2% children had folate deficiency. Baseline B12, folate and tHcy concentrations were similar in the different supplementation groups."

"The participants were families from an ‘extended’ cohort of the PMNS. The PMNS methodology has been reported in detail by Rao et al. (2001)."

"Of these, 119 families remain in follow-up, and the child and parents (349 individuals) were invited to take part in this study."

Comment: 1a. Supplements were similar in appearance with contents known to pharmacist suggesting allocation concealment prior to assignment to clusters. Authors report the use of a random number generation method for randomisation of clusters. Baseline differences in biochemical markers between intervention groups are presented; however, authors report no socio-demographic characteristics at baseline by intervention clusters. Limited information to permit judgment on baseline comparability of clusters.

1b. Authors report a sub-sample of the PMNS cohort was recruited for this study (Figure 1). It is not explicitly stated whether all clusters (families) were identified and consented prior to randomisation. There is indication that families or individuals were recruited post-randomisation; however, the timeline is unclear. No evidence of baseline imbalances across clusters is reported in Table 1 that might suggest differential recruitment.

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quotes: "The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"Of the 119 families (349 individuals) in the extended PMNS cohort, 307 individuals were willing to participate (88% response), 7 (1 pregnant, 6 anemic) were excluded and 300 (106 children, 93 fathers and 101 mothers) were randomized (Figure 1). During the intervention, one woman became pregnant and five participants received B12-containing medication (from family physician) and were excluded from the analysis. Three participants withdrew and one was lost to follow-up after collection of the 4-month sample; they were analyzed using the Last Observation Carried Forward method. Thus, the final analysis includes 294 participants (106 children, 92 fathers and 96 mothers)."

Comments: It is likely that participants were unaware of the composition of supplements received and thus assigned intervention clusters. Trial investigators were blinded to supplement composition and allocated clusters which were revealed after data collection. The intervention was successful for 98% (294/300) of randomised participants within clusters. There is no clear indication that failures occurred in the implementation of the intervention. 

Reasons for loss to follow-up include: pregnancy, receipt of vitamin B12 supplements outside of the intervention, and withdrawal. Other reasons are not reported for withdrawal (n=3) and loss to follow-up (n=1); however, the proportions are small enough to have little to no effect on the outcome. It is not likely that non-adherence may have affected the outcome by cluster.

Comment: Authors report limited information on outcome data available for all eligible and randomised clusters (and specifically for children). Outcome data were available for 16% (48/300) of recruited, eligible and randomised participants. Authors report insufficient information on sensitivity analysis or other analysis methods to assess relationship between missingness of the outcome and its true value. Outcome data are reported for a sub-sample of randomised participants within clusters. Other reasons for missing outcomes include: protocol deviation, pregnancy, withdrawal and loss to follow-up. Reasons reported are unassociated with the true value of the outcome by cluster.

"Detailed physical and biochemical measurements (B12, folate and homocysteine concentrations) and white blood cell counts at baseline and one-year follow-up were measured using standard techniques as described earlier [12]."

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: The present study included children from the Pune Maternal Nutrition Study (PMNS), which was established to examine the relationship between maternal nutrition status, fetal growth and long-term outcomes in the children [13]. "Height was measured to the nearest 0.1cm using a wall mounted stadiometer (CMS Instruments, London, UK) and body weight to the nearest 0.005 kg (Conveigh, Electronic Instruments Ltd, Mumbai, India). "The data are presented as mean and standard deviation (s.d.). Comment: Recruitment for the trial was from 01/04/2007 to 31/03/2008. The trial was registered on 07/09/2007. "Eligible children are allocated by block randomization (block sizes of 8) in a 1:1 ratio to one of the intervention groups. "The baseline features were evenly distributed between the intervention groups. The baseline status of vitamin B12 and its plasma biomarkers were also comparable between the intervention groups (S1 Table)."

Comment: There is indication that a third-party scientist was responsible for generation of random sequence suggesting the allocation sequence was concealed prior to assignment; in addition, vitamin B12 and placebo supplements were similar in appearance and taste. Authors report a random number sequence generation method. There is indication from Table 1 that baseline characteristics were comparable between groups; differences in nutritional status of infants (anaemia, wasting, underweight) may be compatible with chance findings.

The list that linked this identity number to the randomization code was kept with the producers of the supplements and the independent scientist who generated it. None of the investigators had access to this list until the data collection and cleaning for the primary outcomes were completed."

"During weekly visits to the homes, field workers asked the mothers about intake of the paste during the past 7 days and recorded in detail the amount of paste given to the children (i.e., half, one-third, three-fourths, or less)."

"From April 2015 to February 2017, we screened 733 infants and randomized 600 into the study (Fig 1). A total of 26 infants dropped out due to refusal or migration. Two children were unable to complete the end-study activities, leaving 572 infants with complete neurodevelopmental assessments. We were able to collect and analyze blood samples for biomarker assessments at end study from 567 children."

Comments: Based on the trials registry (NCT02272842), blinding is reported as "Masking: Quadruple (Participant, Care Provider, Investigator, Outcomes Assessor)." In addition, there is indication from the published report that participants, investigators and carers delivering the intervention were unaware of assigned groups. Authors report weekly check-ins by field workers regarding supplementation intake and compliance. As a result, there is indication that the intervention was successful for ~95% of subjects. It appears that 26 infants dropped out for personal reasoans and 2 participants were unable to complete study activities. It appears that reasons for loss to follow-up may be unrelated to study non-adherence.

Outcome results are analysed as mean change from baseline to endline and are consistent with the statistical analysis plan.

"Using a factorial design, we randomly assigned eligible children to 1 of 4 treatment groups: 1) placebo (n = 249), 2) 2 times the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)4 of folic acid (n = 249), 3) 2 times the RDA of vitamin B-12 (n = 252), and 4) a combination of both vitamin B-12 and folic acid (n = 250) in blocks of 16. risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:

The treatment allocation was masked to the study participants and the study team throughout the data collection period."

Trials registry (NCT00717730): Masking: Quadruple (Participant, Care Provider, Investigator, Outcomes Assessor).

"Of the randomly assigned children, 99% were available for the last scheduled visit, ie, only 7 children withdrew."

"Compliance was good, and 96% of the scheduled doses were reportedly ingested. "The flow of the participants through the study is shown in Fig 1. Of the 1000 children in the main study, we established contact with 798 children, of whom 791 children consented to participate."

"The study enrolled children from January 2010 to September 2011. Neurodevelopment was added during the first phase as a secondary outcome. Comment: Outcome data were available and analyzed for a sub-sample [~79%; n=791) of 1000 children 6-30 months randomised. risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome

"The Crichton Vocabulary Scales (CVS) covers verbal skills in children 4 to 11 years (17). The CVS is translated to Hindi, with Indian norms providing score a standardized total (18) (Table 1)."

"We calculated a combined WISC-IVINDIA and CVS z score on the basis of converted z scores on each subtest and a combined NEPSY-II z score on the basis of converted z scores in 7 subtests."

"Five psychologists blinded to the intervention groups undertook all assessments after training and standardization in 20 children per tester. The use of a standardised method with quality control measures such as training, and high inter-rater reliability in outcome assessment ensures comparable methods across treatment groups and time points.
