"We present mean (SD) scores for the cognitive tests in the intervention groups. We compared the intervention groups with the placebo group in linear regression models, in which the intervention groups were included as dummy variables and compared against the placebo group."

There is no indication that outcome results are selected from multiple eligible analysis.

"The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"Of the 119 families (349 individuals) in the extended PMNS cohort, 307 individuals were willing to participate (88% response), 7 (1 pregnant, 6 anemic) were excluded and 300 (106 children, 93 fathers and 101 mothers) were randomized (Figure 1). During the intervention, one woman became pregnant and five participants received B12-containing medication (from family physician) and were excluded from the analysis. Three participants withdrew and one was lost to follow-up after collection of the 4-month sample; they were analyzed using the Last Observation Carried Forward method. Thus, the final analysis includes 294 participants (106 children, 92 fathers and 96 mothers)."

Comment: This was a double-blind cluster randomised trial with participants unaware of the composition of supplements received and thus assigned intervention clusters.

Trial investigators were blinded to supplement composition and allocated clusters which were revealed after data collection.

The intervention was successful for 98% (294/300) of randomized participants. There is no clear indication that failures occurred in the implementation of the intervention.

Reasons for loss to follow-up include: pregnancy, receipt of vitamin B12 supplements outside of the intervention, and withdrawal. Other reasons are not reported for withdrawal (n=3) and loss to follow-up (n=1); however, the proportions are small enough to have little to no effect on the outcome. administered in this study: Affect Recognition, Statue and Geometric Puzzles from the Social Perception, Executive Functioning and Visual-Spatial Processing domains, respectively. "Compliance was good, and 96% of the scheduled doses were reportedly ingested. "The flow of the participants through the study is shown in Fig 1. Of the 1000 children in the main study, we established contact with 798 children, of whom 791 children consented to participate."

"The study enrolled children from January 2010 to September 2011. Neurodevelopment was added during the first phase as a secondary outcome. Comment: Outcome data were available and analyzed for a sub-sample [~79%; n=791) of 1000 children 6-30 months randomised. risk-of-bias.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"The unit of randomization was the family, making it a cluster-randomized trial. We stratified the families by the children’s baseline plasma B12 concentrations; those below and above the median value were equally distributed in six groups. Within each group, the statistician randomly allocated codes (A–F) to the participant families."

"Table 1 shows the basic characteristics of the 300 participants. Seventy-two percent fathers, 48% mothers and 27% children were B12 deficient, and 75% fathers, 35% mothers and 47% children were hyperhomocysteinemic. In contrast, only 14% fathers, 8% mothers and 2% children had folate deficiency. Baseline B12, folate and tHcy concentrations were similar in the different supplementation groups."

"The participants were families from an ‘extended’ cohort of the PMNS. The PMNS methodology has been reported in detail by Rao et al. (2001)."

"Of these, 119 families remain in follow-up, and the child and parents (349 individuals) were invited to take part in this study."

Comment: 1a. Supplements were similar in appearance with contents known to pharmacist suggesting allocation concealment prior to assignment to clusters. Authors report the use of a random number generation method for randomisation of clusters. Baseline differences in biochemical markers between intervention groups are presented; however, authors report no socio-demographic characteristics at baseline by intervention clusters. Limited information to permit judgment on baseline comparability of clusters.

1b. Authors report a sub-sample of the PMNS cohort was recruited for this study (Figure 1). It is not explicitly stated whether all clusters (families) were identified and consented prior to randomisation. There is indication that families or individuals were recruited post-randomisation; however, the timeline is unclear. No evidence of baseline imbalances across clusters is reported in Table 1 that might suggest differential recruitment.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The trial was double blinded. We planned to test three levels of B12 supplementation (none, 2 and 10 mg) and each of these at two levels of folic acid supplementation (none and 200 mg), forming six groups (A = B0F0, B = B2F0, C = B10F0, D = B0F200, E = B2F200 and F = B10F200) (Figure 1)."

"The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"Of the 119 families (349 individuals) in the extended PMNS cohort, 307 individuals were willing to participate (88% response), 7 (1 pregnant, 6 anemic) were excluded and 300 (106 children, 93 fathers and 101 mothers) were randomized (Figure 1). During the intervention, one woman became pregnant and five participants received B12-containing medication (from family physician) and were excluded from the analysis. Three participants withdrew and one was lost to follow-up after collection of the 4-month sample; they were analyzed using the Last Observation Carried Forward method. Thus, the final analysis includes 294 participants (106 children, 92 fathers and 96 mothers)."

Comment: This was a double-blind cluster randomised trial with participants unaware of the composition of supplements received and thus assigned intervention clusters.

Trial investigators were blinded to supplement composition and allocated clusters which were revealed after data collection.

The intervention was successful for 98% (294/300) of randomized participants. There is no clear indication that failures occurred in the implementation of the intervention.

Reasons for loss to follow-up include: pregnancy, receipt of vitamin B12 supplements outside of the intervention, and withdrawal. Other reasons are not reported for withdrawal (n=3) and loss to follow-up (n=1); however, the proportions are small enough to have little to no effect on the outcome. It is not likely that non-adherence may have affected the outcome by cluster.

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:

Comment: Authors report limited information on outcome data available for all eligible and randomised clusters (and specifically for children). 

Outcome data were available for 16% (48/300) of recruited, eligible and randomized participants within clusters.

Authors report insufficient information on sensitivity analysis or other analysis methods to assess relationship between missingness of the outcome and its true value.

Outcome data are reported for a sub-sample of randomized participants. Other reasons for missing outcomes include: protocol deviation, pregnancy, withdrawal and loss to follow-up. Reasons reported are unassociated with the true value of the outcome by cluster.

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "Detailed physical and biochemical measurements (B12, folate and homocysteine concentrations) and white blood cell counts at baseline and one-year follow-up were measured using standard techniques as described earlier [12]."

"Digit span test: This test is a measure for working memory and is taken from Malin’s Intelligence Scale for Children. It consists of two parts, forward and backward. The longest digit string recalled is considered as the span [Personal communication]."

"The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. Comment: From author request for unpublished data and study information, there is indication of the use of standardised procedures pertaining to physical assessments including cognitive tests as alluded to by authors. risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The present study included children from the Pune Maternal Nutrition Study (PMNS), which was established to examine the relationship between maternal nutrition status, fetal growth and long-term outcomes in the children [13]. The study design of the B12/ folic acid intervention in the extended PMNS cohort has been described earlier [12]."

"Detailed physical and biochemical measurements (B12, folate and homocysteine concentrations) and white blood cell counts at baseline and one-year follow-up were measured using standard techniques as described earlier [12]."

"The data are presented as mean and standard deviation (s.d.). Though B12 and tHcy concentrations were not normally distributed, we used parametric tests for differences between group means, which are normally distributed as per the central limit theorem.We used analysis of variance to test the differences between supplementation groups, adjusting for the cluster design. There was no difference between clustered and unclustered analysis (statistically insignificant intraclass correlation)."

Comment: Recruitment for the trial was from 01/04/2007 to 31/03/2008. The trial was registered on 07/09/2007. From the trials registry (ISRCTN59289820), the outcome is pre-specified as a secondary outcome measure: "Neuro-cognitive performance* -- to be measured only in children" Outcome reported is in accordance with timepoints and methods reported for other outcomes; no indication of selection from multiple outcome measurements.

Analysis of the outcome reported conforms to the pre-specified analysis plan. There is no clear indication that numerical results were selectively reported from multiple analyses on the basis of the results from allocated clusters.

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "Randomization was concealed, and the study double-masked as the participants were only linked to the intervention through the identity number printed on the supplement labels. The list that linked this identity number to the randomization code was kept with the producers of the supplements and the independent scientist who generated it. None of the investigators had access to this list until the data collection and cleaning for the primary outcomes were completed."

"Eligible children are allocated by block randomization (block sizes of 8) in a 1:1 ratio to one of the intervention groups. The vitamin B12 supplements and placebos have been produced specifically for this trial and are identical in taste and appearance. The supplements or placebos are offered in packages to the enrolled children according to a unique identification number provided by the company."

"The baseline features were evenly distributed between the intervention groups. The baseline status of vitamin B12 and its plasma biomarkers were also comparable between the intervention groups (S1 Table)."

Comment: There is indication that a third-party scientist was responsible for generation of random sequence suggesting the allocation sequence was concealed prior to assignment; in addition, vitamin B12 and placebo supplements were similar in appearance and taste. Authors report a random number sequence generation method. There is indication from Table 1 that baseline characteristics were comparable between groups; differences in nutritional status of infants (anaemia, wasting, underweight) may be compatible with chance findings.

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:

The list that linked this identity number to the randomization code was kept with the producers of the supplements and the independent scientist who generated it. None of the investigators had access to this list until the data collection and cleaning for the primary outcomes were completed."

"During weekly visits to the homes, field workers asked the mothers about intake of the paste during the past 7 days and recorded in detail the amount of paste given to the children (i.e., half, one-third, three-fourths, or less)."

"From April 2015 to February 2017, we screened 733 infants and randomized 600 into the study (Fig 1). A total of 26 infants dropped out due to refusal or migration. Two children were unable to complete the end-study activities, leaving 572 infants with complete neurodevelopmental assessments. We were able to collect and analyze blood samples for biomarker assessments at end study from 567 children."

Comment: Based on the trials registry (NCT02272842), blinding is reported as "Masking : Quadruple (Participant, Care Provider, Investigator, Outcomes Assessor)." In addition, there is indication from the published report that participants, investigators and carers delivering the intervention were unaware of assigned groups. Authors report weekly check-ins by field workers regarding supplementation intake and compliance. As a result, there is indication that the intervention was successful for ~95% of subjects. It appears that 26 infants dropped out for personal reasoans and 2 participants were unable to complete study activities. It appears that reasons for loss to follow-up may be unrelated to study non-adherence.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "From April 2015 to February 2017, we screened 733 infants and randomized 600 into the study (Fig 1). A total of 26 infants dropped out due to refusal or migration. Two children were unable to complete the end-study activities, leaving 572 infants with complete neurodevelopmental assessments. "Among 600 participant infants, we were unable to follow-up on twenty-six participants from the original study mainly due to migration or refusal to participate. Among the 574 children who completed the intervention, we were able to re-consent 555 (96·7 %) at the first scheduled time point and 533 (92·8%) at the second scheduled time point. The main reason for not being re-enrolled in the follow-up rounds was migration (Fig. 1)."

Comment: There is no report of analysis methods to correct for bias or sensitivity analysis under plausible assumptions to ascertain the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value. Thus, there is minimal evidence to suggest that missingness did not bias outcome results. Missingness in outcome occurred due to reasons unrelated to the outcome including migration from prior location and refusal to participate in study.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "WPPSI-IV is a clinical assessment tool of intellectual ability in children aged 2 years and 6 months through 7 years and 7 months (2:6 to 7:7) (22). In addition, we used three indexes: Verbal Comprehension Index, Visual Spatial Index and Working Memory Index. The raw scores of each subscales were converted into index scores and FSIQ scores with an expected mean (SD) of 100 (15)." 

"Before the study start, the team arranged a training workshop in Nepal for the psychologists responsible for assessing children in the study."

"Three study psychologists performed all assessments and quality control. Standardisation exercises were performed in twenty children per tester for each test. We attained an inter-correlation coefficient >98 % for both standardisation and double scoring indicating excellent inter-rater agreement." 

Trials registry (NCT02272842): "Masking : Quadruple (Participant, Care Provider, Investigator, Outcomes Assessor)."

Comment: Outcome measurement conforms to an appropriate and valid method. There is indication that standardised methods involving quality control measures including trained test administrators, pilot exercises, and high inter-rater reliability with expert rater were adopted in outcome assessment ensuring comparable methods across timepoints and treatment groups. None of the investigators had access to this list until the data collection and cleaning for the primary outcomes were completed. It is unclear whether psychologists involved in test administration were blinded; however, there is indication from the trials registry that outcome assessors were blinded to treatment arms.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The main outcomes are changes in growth (z-scores) and in neurodevelopment measured by the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Third Edition, from baseline until the end of the study."

"For the other outcome variables (Bayley-III raw scores, growth, and hemoglobin concentrations), the effects of the intervention were estimated by comparing the changes from baseline to end study between the study groups. The precision of the effect estimates and corresponding values were calculated using the Student t test assuming equal variances."

"Means (SD) and mean differences (95 % CI) for the cognitive outcomes between intervention groups were calculated. In linear regression analyses, we examined the effect of the intervention on the primary outcome (WPPSI-IV FSIQ) in pre-defined subgroups, which were the same as reported in the main paper."

Comment: It is defined as an outcome and its methodology described in the published protocol. Recruitment for the study was from 2015-04-20 to 2024-12-28 and was registered on 2014-10-21. Based on the trials registry (NCT02272842), the outcome is pre-specified as other outcome measures: "Extended Followup Neurodevelopment (IQ)" with "Measure Description - Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence - Fourth Edition. This is a test of general abilities ("IQ-test") Expected mean (SD): 100 (15), higher value indicate better cognitive functioning. Range approx. 40-140" Time Frame is specified as 3 years. Outcome results reported at baseline and at 24 months appear to conform to outcome measurements specified in the study protocol and trials registry. There is minimal indication that outcome resuts are selected based on the results. 

The analyses in this study were carried out according to the predefined protocols and analysis plans. Outcome results are analyzed as mean change from baseline to endline and are consistent with the statistical analysis plan.

"During weekly visits to the homes, field workers asked the mothers about intake of the paste during the past 7 days and recorded in detail the amount of paste given to the children (i.e., half, one-third, three-fourths, or less)."

"From April 2015 to February 2017, we screened 733 infants and randomized 600 into the study (Fig 1). A total of 26 infants dropped out due to refusal or migration. risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"The unit of randomization was the family, making it a cluster-randomized trial. We stratified the families by the children’s baseline plasma B12 concentrations; those below and above the median value were equally distributed in six groups. Within each group, the statistician randomly allocated codes (A–F) to the participant families."

"Table 1 shows the basic characteristics of the 300 participants. Seventy-two percent fathers, 48% mothers and 27% children were B12 deficient, and 75% fathers, 35% mothers and 47% children were hyperhomocysteinemic. In contrast, only 14% fathers, 8% mothers and 2% children had folate deficiency. Baseline B12, folate and tHcy concentrations were similar in the different supplementation groups."

"The participants were families from an ‘extended’ cohort of the PMNS. The PMNS methodology has been reported in detail by Rao et al. (2001)."

"Of these, 119 families remain in follow-up, and the child and parents (349 individuals) were invited to take part in this study."

Comment: 1a. Supplements were similar in appearance with contents known to pharmacist suggesting allocation concealment prior to assignment to clusters. Authors report the use of a random number generation method for randomisation of clusters. Baseline differences in biochemical markers between intervention groups are presented; however, authors report no socio-demographic characteristics at baseline by intervention clusters. Limited information to permit judgment on baseline comparability of clusters.

1b. Authors report a sub-sample of the PMNS cohort was recruited for this study (Figure 1). It is not explicitly stated whether all clusters (families) were identified and consented prior to randomisation. There is indication that families or individuals were recruited post-randomisation; however, the timeline is unclear. No evidence of baseline imbalances across clusters is reported in Table 1 that might suggest differential recruitment.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The trial was double blinded. We planned to test three levels of B12 supplementation (none, 2 and 10 mg) and each of these at two levels of folic acid supplementation (none and 200 mg), forming six groups (A = B0F0, B = B2F0, C = B10F0, D = B0F200, E = B2F200 and F = B10F200) (Figure 1)."

"The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"Of the 119 families (349 individuals) in the extended PMNS cohort, 307 individuals were willing to participate (88% response), 7 (1 pregnant, 6 anemic) were excluded and 300 (106 children, 93 fathers and 101 mothers) were randomized (Figure 1). During the intervention, one woman became pregnant and five participants received B12-containing medication (from family physician) and were excluded from the analysis. Three participants withdrew and one was lost to follow-up after collection of the 4-month sample; they were analyzed using the Last Observation Carried Forward method. Thus, the final analysis includes 294 participants (106 children, 92 fathers and 96 mothers)."

Comment: This was a double-blind cluster randomised trial with participants unaware of the composition of supplements received and thus assigned intervention clusters.

Trial investigators were blinded to supplement composition and allocated clusters which were revealed after data collection.

The intervention was successful for 98% (294/300) of randomized participants. There is no clear indication that failures occurred in the implementation of the intervention.

Reasons for loss to follow-up include: pregnancy, receipt of vitamin B12 supplements outside of the intervention, and withdrawal. Other reasons are not reported for withdrawal (n=3) and loss to follow-up (n=1); however, the proportions are small enough to have little to no effect on the outcome. It is not likely that non-adherence may have affected the outcome by cluster.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:

Comment: Authors report limited information on outcome data available for all eligible and randomized clusters (and specifically for children). 

Outcome data were available for 16% (48/300) of recruited, eligible and randomised participants within clusters.

Authors report insufficient information on sensitivity analysis or other analysis methods to assess relationship between missingness of the outcome and its true value.

Outcome data are reported for a sub-sample of randomised participants. Other reasons for missing outcomes include: protocol deviation, pregnancy, withdrawal and loss to follow-up. Reasons reported are unassociated with the true value of the outcome by cluster.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:

Comment: From author request for unpublished data and study information, there is indication of the use of standardised procedures pertaining to physical assessments including cognitive tests as alluded to by authors. risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The present study included children from the Pune Maternal Nutrition Study (PMNS), which was established to examine the relationship between maternal nutrition status, fetal growth and long-term outcomes in the children [13]. The study design of the B12/ folic acid intervention in the extended PMNS cohort has been described earlier [12]."

"Detailed physical and biochemical measurements (B12, folate and homocysteine concentrations) and white blood cell counts at baseline and one-year follow-up were measured using standard techniques as described earlier [12]."

"The data are presented as mean and standard deviation (s.d.). There was no difference between clustered and unclustered analysis (statistically insignificant intraclass correlation)."

Comment: Recruitment for the trial was from 01/04/2007 to 31/03/2008. The trial was registered on 07/09/2007. From the trials registry (ISRCTN59289820), the outcome is pre-specified as a secondary outcome measure: "Neuro-cognitive performance* -- to be measured only in children" Outcome reported is in accordance with timepoints and methods reported for other outcomes; no indication of selection from multiple outcome measurements.

Analysis of the outcome reported conforms to the pre-specified analysis plan. There is no clear indication that numerical results were selectively reported from multiple analyses on the basis of the results from allocated clusters.

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement: Outcome result judged to be low risk of bias due to low risk in all domains.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote:  "A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp). The intervention was a lipid-based nutritional supplement prepared by NUTRISET Ltd and was provided in jars prelabeled with the subject identification number. The placebo and the vitamin supplements were identical in appearance and taste. The treatment allocation was masked to the study participants and the study team throughout the data collection period."

"Using a factorial design, we randomly assigned eligible children to 1 of 4 treatment groups: 1) placebo (n = 249), 2) 2 times the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)4 of folic acid (n = 249), 3) 2 times the RDA of vitamin B-12 (n = 252), and 4) a combination of both vitamin B-12 and folic acid (n = 250) in blocks of 16. A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp)."

"The baseline features were similar in the 4 groups."

Comment: A third-party scientist was involved in random scheme generation and supplements were similar in appearance suggesting that the allocation sequence may have been concealed prior to assignment. Authors report a random number sequence generation method. Author report and visual inspection of Table 1 suggests no substantial differences in baseline characteristics between treatment groups. Any observable differences are compatible with chance findings.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp). The intervention was a lipid based nutritional supplement prepared by NUTRISET Ltd and was provided in jars prelabeled with the subject identification number. The placebo and the vitamin supplements were identical in appearance and taste. The treatment allocation was masked to the study participants and the study team throughout the data collection period."

Trials registry (NCT00717730): Masking: Quadruple (Participant, Care Provider, Investigator, Outcomes Assessor).

"Of the randomly assigned children, 99% were available for the last scheduled visit, ie, only 7 children withdrew."

"Compliance was good, and 96% of the scheduled doses were reportedly ingested. Compliance was reflected in the change in plasma concentrations of folate, vitamin B-12, and tHcy from baseline to the end of the study (Table 2). At the end of the study, the children who received vitamin B-12 supplements (±folic acid) had a geometric mean vitamin B-12 concentration that was 1.28 times (95% CI: 1.14, 1.44) that of children in the placebo and folic acid groups. Similarly, the geometric mean folate concentration was 3.14 (95% CI: 2.56, 3.86) higher among the folic acid recipients. Either vitamin B-12 or folic acid supplementation alone resulted in a decreased tHcy concentration, with geometric mean ratios of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.72, 0.83) and 0.83 (95% CI: 0.77, 0.89), respectively."

Comment: There is indication from the published report and trials registry that participants, investigators and carers delivering the intervention were blinded to treatment groups. Out of 1000 children 6-30 months randomised, almost all (~99%; 993/1000) participants returned for the last trial visit suggesting the intervention was successful for most participants. Authors report increased ingestion of supplementation with observed changes in vitamin B12, folate and homocysteine concentrations as expected between treatment groups. These observations suggest good adherence to study protocol and unlikely to impact reported outcome.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "Of 1377 eligible children aged 6 to 30 mo, we randomly assigned 1000 children into the study."

"The flow of the participants through the study is shown in Fig 1. Of the 1000 children in the main study, we established contact with 798 children, of whom 791 children consented to participate."

"The study enrolled children from January 2010 to September 2011. Neurodevelopment was added during the first phase as a secondary outcome. We were only able to include the last 422 children for these assessments (10). In September 2016, we attempted to approach all the children in the original trial. Of the 1000 children in the main study, we established contact with 798 children, of whom 791 children consented to participate in the study."

Comment: Outcome data were available and analysed for a sub-sample [~79%; n=791) of 1000 children 6-30 months randomised. Outcome data were analysed in a sub-sample of participants with no analysis methods or sensitivity analysis to ascertain the relationship between the sub-selected outcome data (analysed vs. not re-enroled) and its true value. Authors report only analysing outcome data in a sub-selected sample of randomised children; thus, missingness in the outcome data are unrelated to the true value of the outcome.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quotes: "The Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fourth Edition (India) (WISC-IVINDIA) is an assessment tool of intellectual ability in children validated for the Indian population with Indian norms (16). We conducted 7 subtests that summed up to 3 index scores: Perceptual Reasoning, Processing Speed, and Working Memory (Table 1). We did not conduct tests included in the Verbal Comprehension Index because these tests require English-language skills (16)."

"The Crichton Vocabulary Scales (CVS) covers verbal skills in children 4 to 11 years (17). The CVS is translated to Hindi, with Indian norms providing score a standardized total (18) (Table 1)."

"We calculated a combined WISC-IVINDIA and CVS z score on the basis of converted z scores on each subtest and a combined NEPSY-II z score on the basis of converted z scores in 7 subtests."

"Five psychologists blinded to the intervention groups undertook all assessments after training and standardization in 20 children per tester. Ten percent of all assessments were scored by 2 psychologists, of whom 1 performed the assessments and the other observed and scored. From these double scorings, we attained a coefficient of >96%, indicating excellent interrater agreement."

Trials registry (NCT00717730): Masking: Quadruple (Participant, Care Provider, Investigator, Outcomes Assessor).

Comments: Method used in outcome assessment conforms to a valid and appropriate method for assessing cognitive function using a tool validated for this population. The use of a standardised method with quality control measures such as training, and high inter-rater reliability in outcome assessment ensures comparable methods across treatment groups and time points. Outcome assessors were unaware of treatment group assignments.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quotes: "The study enrolled children from January 2010 to September 2011. Neurodevelopment was added during the first phase as a secondary outcome."

"Scores on the cognitive tests were calculated on the basis of available norms (Table 1). We calculated a combined WISC-IVINDIA and CVS z score on the basis of converted z scores on each subtest and a combined NEPSY-II z score on the basis of converted z scores in 7 subtests (Inhibition-Naming versus Inhibition Contrast Scaled Score, Design Fluency Total Scaled Score, Word Generation-Semantic versus Initial Letter Contrast Scaled Score, Visuomotor Precision Combined Scaled Score, Manual Motor Sequences Total Score [raw score], Affect Recognition Total Scaled Score, and Geometric Puzzles Total Scaled Score)."

"We present mean (SD) scores for the cognitive tests in the intervention groups. We compared the intervention groups with the placebo group in linear regression models, in which the intervention groups were included as dummy variables and compared against the placebo group."

Comments: Recruitment for the trial was from January 2010 to September 2011. Trial (NCT00717730) was registered on 2008-07-16. While the outcome is not specified in the trials registry, there is indication from the published report that the outcome results reported at the 6 to 9 year follow-up period are consistent with a pre-specified analysis plan. Based on the statistical analysis plan, numerical results were reported accordingly as means (SD) at the 6 to 9 year follow-up for all treatment groups. There is no indication that outcome results are selected from multiple eligible analysis.

Quote: "The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"The unit of randomization was the family, making it a cluster-randomized trial. We stratified the families by the children’s baseline plasma B12 concentrations; those below and above the median value were equally distributed in six groups. Within each group, the statistician randomly allocated codes (A–F) to the participant families."

"Table 1 shows the basic characteristics of the 300 participants. Seventy-two percent fathers, 48% mothers and 27% children were B12 deficient, and 75% fathers, 35% mothers and 47% children were hyperhomocysteinemic. In contrast, only 14% fathers, 8% mothers and 2% children had folate deficiency. Baseline B12, folate and tHcy concentrations were similar in the different supplementation groups."

"The participants were families from an ‘extended’ cohort of the PMNS. The PMNS methodology has been reported in detail by Rao et al. (2001)."

"Of these, 119 families remain in follow-up, and the child and parents (349 individuals) were invited to take part in this study."

Comment: 1a. Supplements were similar in appearance with contents known to pharmacist suggesting allocation concealment prior to assignment to clusters. Authors report the use of a random number generation method for randomisation of clusters. Baseline differences in biochemical markers between intervention groups are presented; however, authors report no socio-demographic characteristics at baseline by intervention clusters. There is indication that families or individuals were recruited post-randomisation; however, the timeline is unclear. No evidence of baseline imbalances across clusters is reported in Table 1 that might suggest differential recruitment.

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The trial was double blinded. We planned to test three levels of B12 supplementation (none, 2 and 10 mg) and each of these at two levels of folic acid supplementation (none and 200 mg), forming six groups (A = B0F0, B = B2F0, C = B10F0, D = B0F200, E = B2F200 and F = B10F200) (Figure 1)."

"The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"Of the 119 families (349 individuals) in the extended PMNS cohort, 307 individuals were willing to participate (88% response), 7 (1 pregnant, 6 anemic) were excluded and 300 (106 children, 93 fathers and 101 mothers) were randomized (Figure 1). Comment: This was a double-blind cluster randomised trial with participants unaware of the composition of supplements received and thus assigned intervention clusters.

Quote:  "A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp). The placebo and the vitamin supplements were identical in appearance and taste. The treatment allocation was masked to the study participants and the study team throughout the data collection period."

"Using a factorial design, we randomly assigned eligible children to 1 of 4 treatment groups: 1) placebo (n = 249), 2) 2 times the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)4 of folic acid (n = 249), 3) 2 times the RDA of vitamin B-12 (n = 252), and 4) a combination of both vitamin B-12 and folic acid (n = 250) in blocks of 16. A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp)."

"The baseline features were similar in the 4 groups."

Comment: A third-party scientist was involved in random scheme generation and supplements were similar in appearance suggesting that the allocation sequence may have been concealed prior to assignment. Authors report a random number sequence generation method. Author report and visual inspection of Table 1 suggests no substantial differences in baseline characteristics between treatment groups. Any observable differences are compatible with chance findings.

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:

The placebo and the vitamin supplements were identical in appearance and taste. The treatment allocation was masked to the study participants and the study team throughout the data collection period."

Trials registry (NCT00717730): Masking: Quadruple (Participant, Care Provider, Investigator, Outcomes Assessor).

"Of the randomly assigned children, 99% were available for the last scheduled visit, ie, only 7 children withdrew."

"Compliance was good, and 96% of the scheduled doses were reportedly ingested. Compliance was reflected in the change in plasma concentrations of folate, vitamin B-12, and tHcy from baseline to the end of the study (Table 2). At the end of the study, the children who received vitamin B-12 supplements (±folic acid) had a geometric mean vitamin B-12 concentration that was 1.28 times (95% CI: 1.14, 1.44) that of children in the placebo and folic acid groups. Similarly, the geometric mean folate concentration was 3.14 (95% CI: 2.56, 3.86) higher among the folic acid recipients. Either vitamin B-12 or folic acid supplementation alone resulted in a decreased tHcy concentration, with geometric mean ratios of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.72, 0.83) and 0.83 (95% CI: 0.77, 0.89), respectively."

Comment: There is indication from the published report and trials registry that participants, investigators and carers delivering the intervention were blinded to treatment groups. Out of 1000 children 6-30 months randomised, almost all (~99%; 993/1000) participants returned for the last trial visit suggesting the intervention was successful for most participants. Authors report increased ingestion of supplementation with observed changes in vitamin B12, folate and homocysteine concentrations as expected between treatment groups. These observations suggest good adherence to study protocol and unlikely to impact reported outcome.

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "Of 1377 eligible children aged 6 to 30 mo, we randomly assigned 1000 children into the study."

"The flow of the participants through the study is shown in Fig 1. Of the 1000 children in the main study, we established contact with 798 children, of whom 791 children consented to participate."

"The study enrolled children from January 2010 to September 2011. Neurodevelopment was added during the first phase as a secondary outcome. We were only able to include the last 422 children for these assessments (10). In September 2016, we attempted to approach all the children in the original trial. Of the 1000 children in the main study, we established contact with 798 children, of whom 791 children consented to participate in the study."

Comment: Outcome data were available and analysed for a sub-sample [~79%; n=791) of 1000 children 6-30 months randomised. Outcome data were analyzed in a sub-sample of participants with no analysis methods or sensitivity to ascertain the relationship between the sub-selected outcome data (analysed vs. not re-enroled) and its true value. Authors report only analysing outcome data in a sub-selected sample of randomised children; thus, missingness in the outcome data are unrelated to the true value of the outcome.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fourth Edition (India) (WISC-IVINDIA) is an assessment tool of intellectual ability in children validated for the Indian population with Indian norms (16). We conducted 7 subtests that summed up to 3 index scores: Perceptual Reasoning, Processing Speed, and Working Memory (Table 1). We did not conduct tests included in the Verbal Comprehension Index because these tests require English-language skills (16)."

"The Crichton Vocabulary Scales (CVS) covers verbal skills in children 4 to 11 years (17). The CVS is translated to Hindi, with Indian norms providing score a standardized total (18) (Table 1)."

"We calculated a combined WISC-IVINDIA and CVS z score on the basis of converted z scores on each subtest and a combined NEPSY-II z score on the basis of converted z scores in 7 subtests."

"Five psychologists blinded to the intervention groups undertook all assessments after training and standardization in 20 children per tester. Ten percent of all assessments were scored by 2 psychologists, of whom 1 performed the assessments and the other observed and scored. From these double scorings, we attained a coefficient of >96%, indicating excellent interrater agreement."

Trials registry (NCT00717730): Masking: Quadruple (Participant, Care Provider, Investigator, Outcomes Assessor).

Comment: Method used in outcome assessment conforms to a valid and appropriate method for assessing cognitive function using a tool validated for this population. The use of a standardised method with quality control measures such as training, and high inter-rater reliability in outcome assessment ensures comparable methods across treatment groups and time points. Outcome assessors were unaware of treatment group assignments.

"Scores on the cognitive tests were calculated on the basis of available norms (Table 1). We calculated a combined WISC-IVINDIA and CVS z score on the basis of converted z scores on each subtest and a combined NEPSY-II z score on the basis of converted z scores in 7 subtests (Inhibition-Naming versus Inhibition Contrast Scaled Score, Design Fluency Total Scaled Score,
Word Generation-Semantic versus Initial Letter Contrast Scaled Score, Visuomotor Precision Combined Scaled Score, Manual Motor Sequences Total Score [raw score], Affect Recognition Total Scaled Score, and Geometric Puzzles Total Scaled Score)."

"We present mean (SD) scores for the cognitive tests in the intervention groups. We compared the intervention groups with the placebo group in linear regression models, in which the intervention groups were included as dummy variables and compared against the placebo group."

Comment: Recruitment for the trial was from January 2010 to September 2011. Trial (NCT00717730) was registered on 2008-07-16. In trials registry (CTRI/2016/11/007494), it is defined as an outcome to be measured at enrolment (5-6 years after supplementation) but limited information is provided. While the outcome is not specified in the trials registry, there is indication from the published report that the outcome results reported at the 6 to 9 year follow-up period are consistent with a pre-specified analysis plan. Based on the statistical analysis plan, numerical results were reported accordingly as means (SD) at the 6 to 9 year follow-up for all treatment groups. There is no indication that outcome results are selected from multiple eligible analysis.

"The baseline features were evenly distributed between the intervention groups. The baseline status of vitamin B12 and its plasma biomarkers were also comparable between the intervention groups (S1 Table)."

Quote: "The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"The unit of randomization was the family, making it a cluster-randomized trial. We stratified the families by the children’s baseline plasma B12 concentrations; those below and above the median value were equally distributed in six groups. Within each group, the statistician randomly allocated codes (A–F) to the participant families."

"Table 1 shows the basic characteristics of the 300 participants. Seventy-two percent fathers, 48% mothers and 27% children were B12 deficient, and 75% fathers, 35% mothers and 47% children were hyperhomocysteinemic. In contrast, only 14% fathers, 8% mothers and 2% children had folate deficiency. Baseline B12, folate and tHcy concentrations were similar in the different supplementation groups."

"The participants were families from an ‘extended’ cohort of the PMNS. The PMNS methodology has been reported in detail by Rao et al. (2001)."

"Of these, 119 families remain in follow-up, and the child and parents (349 individuals) were invited to take part in this study."

Comment: 1a. Supplements were similar in appearance with contents known to pharmacist suggesting allocation concealment prior to assignment to clusters. Authors report the use of a random number generation method for randomisation of clusters. Baseline differences in biochemical markers between intervention groups are presented; however, authors report no socio-demographic characteristics at baseline by intervention clusters. Limited information to permit judgment on baseline comparability of clusters.

1b. Authors report a sub-sample of the PMNS cohort was recruited for this study (Figure 1). It is not explicitly stated whether all clusters (families) were identified and consented prior to randomisation. There is indication that families or individuals were recruited post-randomisation; however, the timeline is unclear. No evidence of baseline imbalances across clusters is reported in Table 1 that might suggest differential recruitment.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The trial was double blinded. We planned to test three levels of B12 supplementation (none, 2 and 10 mg) and each of these at two levels of folic acid supplementation (none and 200 mg), forming six groups (A = B0F0, B = B2F0, C = B10F0, D = B0F200, E = B2F200 and F = B10F200) (Figure 1)."

"The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"Of the 119 families (349 individuals) in the extended PMNS cohort, 307 individuals were willing to participate (88% response), 7 (1 pregnant, 6 anemic) were excluded and 300 (106 children, 93 fathers and 101 mothers) were randomized (Figure 1). During the intervention, one woman became pregnant and five participants received B12-containing medication (from family physician) and were excluded from the analysis. Three participants withdrew and one was lost to follow-up after collection of the 4-month sample; they were analyzed using the Last Observation Carried Forward method. Thus, the final analysis includes 294 participants (106 children, 92 fathers and 96 mothers)."

Comment: This was a double-blind cluster randomised trial with participants unaware of the composition of supplements received and thus assigned intervention clusters.

Trial investigators were blinded to supplement composition and allocated clusters which were revealed after data collection.

The intervention was successful for 98% (294/300) of randomised participants within clusters. There is no clear indication that failures occurred in the implementation of the intervention.

Reasons for loss to follow-up include: pregnancy, receipt of vitamin B12 supplements outside of the intervention, and withdrawal. Other reasons are not reported for withdrawal (n=3) and loss to follow-up (n=1); however, the proportions are small enough to have little to no effect on the outcome. It is not likely that non-adherence may have affected the outcome by cluster.

Outcome data were available for 16% (48/300) of recruited, eligible and randomised participants within clusters.

Authors report insufficient information on sensitivity analysis or other analysis methods to assess relationship between missingness of the outcome and its true value.

Outcome data are reported for a sub-sample of randomised participants within clusters. Other reasons for missing outcomes include: protocol deviation, pregnancy, withdrawal and loss to follow-up. Reasons reported are unassociated with the true value of the outcome by cluster.

Quote: "The trial was double blinded. We planned to test three levels of B12 supplementation (none, 2 and 10 mg) and each of these at two levels of folic acid supplementation (none and 200 mg), forming six groups (A = B0F0, B = B2F0, C = B10F0, D = B0F200, E = B2F200 and F = B10F200) (Figure 1)."

"The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"Of the 119 families (349 individuals) in the extended PMNS cohort, 307 individuals were willing to participate (88% response), 7 (1 pregnant, 6 anemic) were excluded and 300 (106 children, 93 fathers and 101 mothers) were randomized (Figure 1). Quote: "The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"The unit of randomization was the family, making it a cluster-randomized trial. We stratified the families by the children’s baseline plasma B12 concentrations; those below and above the median value were equally distributed in six groups. Within each group, the statistician randomly allocated codes (A–F) to the participant families."

"Table 1 shows the basic characteristics of the 300 participants. Seventy-two percent fathers, 48% mothers and 27% children were B12 deficient, and 75% fathers, 35% mothers and 47% children were hyperhomocysteinemic. In contrast, only 14% fathers, 8% mothers and 2% children had folate deficiency. Baseline B12, folate and tHcy concentrations were similar in the different supplementation groups."

"The participants were families from an ‘extended’ cohort of the PMNS. The PMNS methodology has been reported in detail by Rao et al. (2001)."

"Of these, 119 families remain in follow-up, and the child and parents (349 individuals) were invited to take part in this study."

Comment: 1a. Supplements were similar in appearance with contents known to pharmacist suggesting allocation concealment prior to assignment to clusters. Authors report the use of a random number generation method for randomisation of clusters. Baseline differences in biochemical markers between intervention groups are presented; however, authors report no socio-demographic characteristics at baseline by intervention clusters. Limited information to permit judgment on baseline comparability of clusters.

1b. Authors report a sub-sample of the PMNS cohort was recruited for this study (Figure 1). It is not explicitly stated whether all clusters (families) were identified and consented prior to randomisation. There is indication that families or individuals were recruited post-randomisation; however, the timeline is unclear. No evidence of baseline imbalances across clusters is reported in Table 1 that might suggest differential recruitment.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The trial was double blinded. We planned to test three levels of B12 supplementation (none, 2 and 10 mg) and each of these at two levels of folic acid supplementation (none and 200 mg), forming six groups (A = B0F0, B = B2F0, C = B10F0, D = B0F200, E = B2F200 and F = B10F200) (Figure 1)."

"The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"Of the 119 families (349 individuals) in the extended PMNS cohort, 307 individuals were willing to participate (88% response), 7 (1 pregnant, 6 anemic) were excluded and 300 (106 children, 93 fathers and 101 mothers) were randomized (Figure 1). During the intervention, one woman became pregnant and five participants received B12-containing medication (from family physician) and were excluded from the analysis. Three participants withdrew and one was lost to follow-up after collection of the 4-month sample; they were analyzed using the Last Observation Carried Forward method. Thus, the final analysis includes 294 participants (106 children, 92 fathers and 96 mothers)."

Comment: This was a double-blind cluster randomised trial with participants unaware of the composition of supplements received and thus assigned intervention clusters.

Trial investigators were blinded to supplement composition and allocated clusters which were revealed after data collection.

The intervention was successful for 98% (294/300) of randomised participants within clusters. There is no clear indication that failures occurred in the implementation of the intervention.

Reasons for loss to follow-up include: pregnancy, receipt of vitamin B12 supplements outside of the intervention, and withdrawal. Other reasons are not reported for withdrawal (n=3) and loss to follow-up (n=1); however, the proportions are small enough to have little to no effect on the outcome. It is not likely that non-adherence may have affected the outcome by cluster.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "Of the 119 families (349 individuals) in the extended PMNS cohort, 307 individuals were willing to participate (88% response), 7 (1 pregnant, 6 anemic) were excluded and 300 (106 children, 93 fathers and 101 mothers) were randomized (Figure 1). During the intervention, one woman became pregnant and five participants received B12-containing medication (from family physician) and were excluded from the analysis. Three participants withdrew and one was lost to follow-up after collection of the 4-month sample; they were analyzed using the Last Observation Carried Forward method. Thus, the final analysis includes 294 participants (106 children, 92 fathers and 96 mothers)." 

"In brief, 119 families (parents and children trios) from the extended PMNS were randomized in groups and supplemented daily for 12 months with B12 (10 µg) and/or folic acid (200 µg), to investigate their effect on plasma homocysteine levels. We randomly selected 12 children (out of a total 15–17 children per group) from each of the four supplementation groups – placebo (B0F0), folic acid (B0F200), B12 (B10F0), B12 + folic acid acid (B10F200), and compared their methylome before and after supplementation (Figure 1)."

Comment: Authors report limited information on outcome data available for all eligible and randomised clusters (and specifically for children). Outcome data were available for 16% (48/300) of recruited, eligible and randomised participants within clusters. Authors report insufficient information on sensitivity analysis or other analysis methods to assess relationship between missingness of the outcome and its true value.

Outcome data are reported for a sub-sample of randomised participants. Other reasons for missing outcomes include: protocol deviation, pregnancy, withdrawal and loss to follow-up. Reasons reported are unassociated with the true value of the outcome by cluster.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "Detailed physical and biochemical measurements (B12, folate and homocysteine concentrations) and white blood cell counts at baseline and one-year follow-up were measured using standard techniques as described earlier [12]."

Raven’s Color Progressive Matrices (CPM): It is a measure of intelligence designed for young children which measures ability to think and perceive. The test consists of 36 items in 3 sets, each set containing 12 items. The number of correct responses is the measure of performance [personal communication]. 

"The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

Comment: From author request for unpublished data and study information, there is indication of the use of standardised procedures pertaining to physical assessments including cognitive tests as alluded to by authors. Limited information is reported on blinding of outcome assessors; however, only a third-party pharmacist was aware of supplement composition, suggesting that trial investigators and research personnel were likely blinded to intervention cluster allocations.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: The present study included children from the Pune Maternal Nutrition Study (PMNS), which was established to examine the relationship between maternal nutrition status, fetal growth and long-term outcomes in the children [13]. The study design of the B12/ folic acid intervention in the extended PMNS cohort has been described earlier [12].

"The data are presented as mean and standard deviation (s.d.). Though B12 and tHcy concentrations were not normally distributed, we used parametric tests for differences between group means, which are normally distributed as per the central limit theorem.We used analysis of variance to test the differences between supplementation groups, adjusting for the cluster design. There was no difference between clustered and unclustered analysis (statistically insignificant intraclass correlation)."

Comment: Recruitment for the trial was from 01/04/2007 to 31/03/2008. The trial was registered on 07/09/2007. From the trials registry (ISRCTN59289820), the outcome is pre-specified as a secondary outcome measure: "Neuro-cognitive performance* -- to be measured only in children." Outcome reported is in accordance with timepoints and methods reported for other outcomes; no indication of selection from multiple outcome measurements.

Analysis of the outcome reported conforms to the pre-specified analysis plan. There is no clear indication that numerical results were selectively reported from multiple analyses on the basis of the results from allocated clusters.

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement: Outcome result judged to be at low risk of bias due to low risk in all domains.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "Randomization was concealed, and the study double-masked as the participants were only linked to the intervention through the identity number printed on the supplement labels. The list that linked this identity number to the randomization code was kept with the producers of the supplements and the independent scientist who generated it. None of the investigators had access to this list until the data collection and cleaning for the primary outcomes were completed."

"Eligible children are allocated by block randomization (block sizes of 8) in a 1:1 ratio to one of the intervention groups. The vitamin B12 supplements and placebos have been produced specifically for this trial and are identical in taste and appearance. The supplements or placebos are offered in packages to the enrolled children according to a unique identification number provided by the company."

"The baseline features were evenly distributed between the intervention groups. The baseline status of vitamin B12 and its plasma biomarkers were also comparable between the intervention groups (S1 Table)."

Comment: There is indication that a third-party scientist was responsible for generation of random sequence suggesting the allocation sequence was concealed prior to assignment; in addition, vitamin B12 and placebo supplements were similar in appearance and taste. Authors report a random number sequence generation method. There is indication from Table 1 that baseline characteristics were comparable between groups; differences in nutritional status of infants (anaemia, wasting, underweight) may be compatible with chance findings.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "Randomization was concealed, and the study double-masked as the participants were only linked to the intervention through the identity number printed on the supplement labels. The list that linked this identity number to the randomization code was kept with the producers of the supplements and the independent scientist who generated it. None of the investigators had access to this list until the data collection and cleaning for the primary outcomes were completed."

"During weekly visits to the homes, field workers asked the mothers about intake of the paste during the past 7 days and recorded in detail the amount of paste given to the children (i.e., half, one-third, three-fourths, or less)."

"From April 2015 to February 2017, we screened 733 infants and randomized 600 into the study (Fig 1). A total of 26 infants dropped out due to refusal or migration. Two children were unable to complete the end-study activities, leaving 572 infants with complete neurodevelopmental assessments. We were able to collect and analyze blood samples for biomarker assessments at end study from 567 children."

Comment: Based on the trials registry (NCT02272842), blinding is reported as "Masking : Quadruple (Participant, Care Provider, Investigator, Outcomes Assessor)." In addition, there is indication from the published report that participants, investigators and carers delivering the intervention were unaware of assigned groups. Authors report weekly check-ins by field workers regarding supplementation intake and compliance. As a result, there is indication that the intervention was successful for ~95% of subjects. It appears that 26 infants dropped out for personal reasoans and 2 participants were unable to complete study activities. It appears that reasons for loss to follow-up may be unrelated to study non-adherence.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "From April 2015 to February 2017, we screened 733 infants and randomized 600 into the study (Fig 1). A total of 26 infants dropped out due to refusal or migration. Two children were unable to complete the end-study activities, leaving 572 infants with complete neurodevelopmental assessments. We were able to collect and analyze blood samples for biomarker assessments at end study from 567 children."

"Among 600 participant infants, we were unable to follow-up on twenty-six participants from the original study mainly due to migration or refusal to participate. Among the 574 children who completed the intervention, we were able to re-consent 555 (96·7 %) at the first scheduled time point and 533 (92·8%) at the second scheduled time point. The main reason for not being re-enrolled in the follow-up rounds was migration (Fig. 1)."

Comment: There is no report of analysis methods to correct for bias or sensitivity analysis under plausible assumptions to ascertain the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value. Thus, there is minimal evidence to suggest that missingness did not bias outcome results. Missingness in outcome occurred due to reasons unrelated to the outcome including migration from prior location and refusal to participate in study.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "WPPSI-IV is a clinical assessment tool of intellectual ability in children aged 2 years and 6 months through 7 years and 7 months (2:6 to 7:7) (22). We used six subtests; Receptive vocabulary, Block Design, Picture Memory, Object Assembly, Zoo Locations and Information to generate standardised composite scores for the FSIQ. In addition, we used three indexes: Verbal Comprehension Index, Visual Spatial Index and Working Memory Index. The raw scores of each subscales were converted into index scores and FSIQ scores with an expected mean (SD) of 100 (15)." 

"Before the study start, the team arranged a training workshop in Nepal for the psychologists responsible for assessing children in the study."

"Three study psychologists performed all assessments and quality control. Standardisation exercises were performed in twenty children per tester for each test. Double scoring was done throughout the study in 10 %of all assessments by two psychologists. We attained an inter-correlation coefficient >98 % for both standardisation and double scoring indicating excellent inter-rater agreement." 

Trials registry (NCT02272842): "Masking: Quadruple (Participant, Care Provider, Investigator, Outcomes Assessor)."

Comment: Outcome measurement conforms to an appropriate and valid method. There is indication that standardised methods involving quality control measures including trained test administrators, pilot exercises, and high inter-rater reliability with expert rater were adopted in outcome assessment ensuring comparable methods across timepoints and treatment groups. None of the investigators had access to this list until the data collection and cleaning for the primary outcomes were completed. It is unclear whether psychologists involved in test administration were blinded; however, there is indication from the trials registry that outcome assessors were blinded to treatment arms.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The main outcomes are changes in growth (z-scores) and in neurodevelopment measured by the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Third Edition, from baseline until the end of the study."

"For the other outcome variables (Bayley-III raw scores, growth, and hemoglobin concentrations), the effects of the intervention were estimated by comparing the changes from baseline to end study between the study groups. The precision of the effect estimates and corresponding values were calculated using the Student t test assuming equal variances."

"In the first follow-up, when the children were 30–35 months old, they were assessed with the Bayley-III. In the second follow-up at 42–47 months, children were assessed using the WPPSI-IV and the Neuropsychological Assessment, 2nd edition (NEPSY-II). "

"Means (SD) and mean differences (95 % CI) for the cognitive outcomes between intervention groups were calculated. In linear regression analyses, we examined the effect of the intervention on the primary outcome (WPPSI-IV FSIQ) in pre-defined subgroups, which were the same as reported in the main paper."

Comment: It is defined as an outcome and its methodology described in the published protocol. Recruitment for the study was from 2015-04-20 to 2024-12-28 and was registered on 2014-10-21. Based on the trials registry (NCT02272842), the outcome is pre-specified as other outcome measures: "Extended Followup Neurodevelopment (IQ)" with "Measure Description - Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence - Fourth Edition. This is a test of general abilities ("IQ-test") Expected mean (SD): 100 (15), higher value indicate better cognitive functioning. Range approx. 40-140" Time Frame is specified as 3 years. Outcome results reported at baseline and at 24 months appear to conform to outcome measurements specified in the study protocol and trials registry. There is minimal indication that outcome resuts are selected based on the results. 

The analyses in this study were carried out according to the predefined protocols and analysis plans. Outcome results are analyzed as mean change from baseline to endline and are consistent with the statistical analysis plan.

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote:  "A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp). The intervention was a lipid-based nutritional supplement prepared by NUTRISET Ltd and was provided in jars prelabeled with the subject identification number. The placebo and the vitamin supplements were identical in appearance and taste. The treatment allocation was masked to the study participants and the study team throughout the data collection period."

"Using a factorial design, we randomly assigned eligible children to 1 of 4 treatment groups: 1) placebo (n = 249), 2) 2 times the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)4 of folic acid (n = 249), 3) 2 times the RDA of vitamin B-12 (n = 252), and 4) a combination of both vitamin B-12 and folic acid (n = 250) in blocks of 16. A scientist at the University of Bergen, who was otherwise not involved in the study, provided the randomization scheme by using Stata Version 10 (StataCorp)."

"The baseline features were similar in the 4 groups."

Comment: A third-party scientist was involved in random scheme generation and supplements were similar in appearance suggesting that the allocation sequence may have been concealed prior to assignment. Authors report a random number sequence generation method. Author report and visual inspection of Table 1 suggests no substantial differences in baseline characteristics between treatment groups. Any observable differences are compatible with chance findings.

The intervention was a lipid based nutritional supplement prepared by NUTRISET Ltd and was provided in jars prelabeled with the subject identification number. The placebo and the vitamin supplements were identical in appearance and taste. The treatment allocation was masked to the study participants and the study team throughout the data collection period."

Trials registry (NCT00717730): Masking: Quadruple (Participant, Care Provider, Investigator, Outcomes Assessor).

"Of the randomly assigned children, 99% were available for the last scheduled visit, ie, only 7 children withdrew."

"Compliance was good, and 96% of the scheduled doses were reportedly ingested. Compliance was reflected in the change in plasma concentrations of folate, vitamin B-12, and tHcy from baseline to the end of the study (Table 2). At the end of the study, the children who received vitamin B-12 supplements (± folic acid) had a geometric mean vitamin B-12 concentration that was 1.28 times (95% CI: 1.14, 1.44) that of children in the placebo and folic acid groups. Similarly, the geometric mean folate concentration was 3.14 (95% CI: 2.56, 3.86) higher among the folic acid recipients. Either vitamin B-12 or folic acid supplementation alone resulted in a decreased tHcy concentration, with geometric mean ratios of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.72, 0.83) and 0.83 (95% CI: 0.77, 0.89), respectively."

Comment: There is indication from the published report and trials registry that participants, investigators and carers delivering the intervention were blinded to treatment groups. Out of 1000 children 6-30 months randomised, almost all (~99%; 993/1000) participants returned for the last trial visit suggesting the intervention was successful for most participants. Authors report increased ingestion of supplementation with observed changes in vitamin B12, folate and homocysteine concentrations as expected between treatment groups. These observations suggest good adherence to study protocol and unlikely to impact reported outcome.

"The flow of the participants through the study is shown in Fig 1. Of the 1000 children in the main study, we established contact with 798 children, of whom 791 children consented to participate."

"The study enrolled children from January 2010 to September 2011. Neurodevelopment was added during the first phase as a secondary outcome. We were only able to include the last 422 children for these assessments (10). In September 2016, we attempted to approach all the children in the original trial. Of the 1000 children in the main study, we established contact with 798 children, of whom 791 children consented to participate in the study."

Comment: Outcome data were available and analysed for a sub-sample [~79%; n=791) of 1000 children 6-30 months randomised. Outcome data were analysed in a sub-sample of participants with no analysis methods or sensitivity methods to ascertain the relationship between the sub-selected outcome data (analysed vs. not re-enroled) and its true value. Authors report only analysing outcome data in a sub-selected sample of randomized children; thus, missingness in the outcome data are unrelated to the true value of the outcome.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fourth Edition (India) (WISC-IVINDIA) is an assessment tool of intellectual ability in children validated for the Indian population with Indian norms (16). We conducted 7 subtests that summed up to 3 index scores: Perceptual Reasoning, Processing Speed, and Working Memory (Table 1). We did not conduct tests included in the Verbal Comprehension Index because these tests require English-language skills (16)."

"The Crichton Vocabulary Scales (CVS) covers verbal skills in children 4 to 11 years (17). The CVS is translated to Hindi, with Indian norms providing score a standardized total (18) (Table 1)."

"We calculated a combined WISC-IVINDIA and CVS z score on the basis of converted z scores on each subtest and a combined NEPSY-II z score on the basis of converted z scores in 7 subtests."

"Five psychologists blinded to the intervention groups undertook all assessments after training and standardization in 20 children per tester. Ten percent of all assessments were scored by 2 psychologists, of whom 1 performed the assessments and the other observed and scored. From these double scorings, we attained a coefficient of >96%, indicating excellent interrater agreement."

Trials registry (NCT00717730): Masking: Quadruple (Participant, Care Provider, Investigator, Outcomes Assessor).

Comment: Method used in outcome assessment conforms to a valid and appropriate method for assessing cognitive function using a tool validated for this population. The use of a standardised method with quality control measures such as training, and high inter-rater reliability in outcome assessment ensures comparable methods across treatment groups and time points. Outcome assessors were unaware of treatment group assignments.

While the outcome is not specified in the trials registry, there is indication from the published report that the outcome results reported at the 6 to 9 year follow-up period are consistent with a pre-specified analysis plan. Based on the statistical analysis plan, numerical results were reported accordingly as means (SD) at the 6 to 9 year follow-up for all treatment groups.
