"Using a factorial design, we randomly assigned eligible children to 1 of 4 treatment groups: 1) placebo (n = 249), 2) 2 times the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)4 of folic acid (n = 249), 3) 2 times the RDA of vitamin B-12 (n = 252), and 4) a combination of both vitamin B-12 and folic acid (n = 250) in blocks of 16. "The baseline features were similar in the 4 groups."

Comment: A third-party scientist was involved in random scheme generation and supplements were similar in appearance suggesting that the allocation sequence may have been concealed prior to assignment. risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "Ensuring double blinding, the placebo and the vitamin supplements were identical in appearance and taste and the allocation was masked to the participants as well as the study team throughout the data collection period."

"Of the randomly assigned children, 99% were available for the last scheduled visit, ie, only 7 children withdrew."

"Compliance was good, and 96% of the scheduled doses were reportedly ingested. "The ASQ-3 scores for the total sample are presented as means (SD). Comment: Limited information on analysis in sub-sample from trials registry and study protocol. However, recruitment for the trial was from January 2010 to September 2011. Based on the statistical analysis plan, numerical results were reported accordingly as means (SD) at baseline and at the end of the study for all treatment groups. There is no indication that outcome results are selected from multiple eligible analysis.

Quote: "The contents of the capsules were known only to the pharmacist until the end of the trial. The codes were revealed only after data analysis. The study capsules were manufactured in six different colors. The supplements were dispensed monthly in containers labeled with the participant’s name and capsule group (A–F). All members of the family received the same colored capsules."

"The unit of randomization was the family, making it a cluster-randomized trial. We stratified the families by the children’s baseline plasma B12 concentrations; those below and above the median value were equally distributed in six groups. Within each group, the statistician randomly allocated codes (A–F) to the participant families."

"Table 1 shows the basic characteristics of the 300 participants. Seventy-two percent fathers, 48% mothers and 27% children were B12 deficient, and 75% fathers, 35% mothers and 47% children were hyperhomocysteinemic. In contrast, only 14% fathers, 8% mothers and 2% children had folate deficiency. Baseline B12, folate and tHcy concentrations were similar in the different supplementation groups."

"The participants were families from an ‘extended’ cohort of the PMNS. The PMNS methodology has been reported in detail by Rao et al. (2001)."

"Of these, 119 families remain in follow-up, and the child and parents (349 individuals) were invited to take part in this study."

Comment: 1a. Supplements were similar in appearance with contents known to pharmacist suggesting allocation concealment prior to assignment to clusters. Authors report the use of a random number generation method for randomisation of clusters. Baseline differences in biochemical markers between intervention groups are presented; however, authors report no socio-demographic characteristics at baseline by intervention clusters. Limited information to permit judgment on baseline comparability of clusters.

1b. Authors report a sub-sample of the PMNS cohort was recruited for this study (Figure 1). It is not explicitly stated whether all clusters (families) were identified and consented prior to randomisation. There is indication that families or individuals were recruited post-randomisation; however, the timeline is unclear. No evidence of baseline imbalances across clusters is reported in Table 1 that might suggest differential recruitment.

"Of the 119 families (349 individuals) in the extended PMNS cohort, 307 individuals were willing to participate (88% response), 7 (1 pregnant, 6 anemic) were excluded and 300 (106 children, 93 fathers and 101 mothers) were randomized (Figure 1). Comment: It is likely that participants were unaware of the composition of supplements received and thus assigned intervention clusters.

Trial investigators were blinded to supplement composition and allocated groups which were revealed after data collection.

Reasons for loss to follow-up include: pregnancy, receipt of vitamin B12 supplements outside of the intervention, and withdrawal. Other reasons are not reported for withdrawal (n=3) and loss to follow-up (n=1); however, the proportions are small enough to have little to no effect on the outcome. It is not likely that non-adherence may have affected the outcome by cluster.

The treatment allocation was masked to the study participants and the study team throughout the data collection period."

"Using a factorial design, we randomly assigned eligible children to 1 of 4 treatment groups: 1) placebo (n = 249), 2) 2 times the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)4 of folic acid (n = 249), 3) 2 times the RDA of vitamin B-12 (n = 252), and 4) a combination of both vitamin B-12 and folic acid (n = 250) in blocks of 16. "The baseline features were similar in the 4 groups."

Comment: A third-party scientist was involved in random scheme generation and supplements were similar in appearance suggesting that the allocation sequence may have been concealed prior to assignment. Authors report a random number sequence generation method. Author report and visual inspection of Table 1 suggests no substantial differences in baseline characteristics between treatment groups. Any observable differences are compatible with chance findings.

"Of 1377 eligible children aged 6230 mo, we randomly assigned 1000 children into the study."

Outcome data were analysed and available for a sub-sample (n=256) of 1000 children 6-30 months randomised.

"The participants were families from an ‘extended’ cohort of the PMNS. The PMNS methodology has been reported in detail by Rao et al. (2001)."

"Of these, 119 families remain in follow-up, and the child and parents (349 individuals) were invited to take part in this study."

Comment: 1a. Supplements were similar in appearance with contents known to pharmacist suggesting allocation concealment prior to assignment to clusters. Authors report the use of a random number generation method for randomisation of clusters. Baseline differences in biochemical markers between intervention groups are presented; however, authors report no socio-demographic characteristics at baseline by intervention clusters. Limited information to permit judgment on baseline comparability of clusters.

It is not explicitly stated whether all clusters (families) were identified and consented prior to randomisation. There is indication that families or individuals were recruited post-randomisation; however, the timeline is unclear. No evidence of baseline imbalances across clusters is reported in Table 1 that might suggest differential recruitment.

The analyses are restricted to the group with both baseline and end-of-study blood samples, i.e., a total of 262 children."

"Blood samples from 10 children could not be collected since the family refused or because they had left the area at the time of blood sample, leaving a total of 262 children with blood sample data at the end of the study."

"The present findings come from a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled preventive field trial with a factorial design that evaluated the impact of supplementation with folic acid, vitamin B12, or both on childhood infections [12]. The analyses are restricted to the group with both baseline and end-of-study blood samples, i.e., a total of 262 children."

"A total of 272 children were assigned for blood sampling at the end of the study, equally distributed among the 4 treatments groups through a randomization process. Blood samples from 10 children could not be collected since the family refused or because they had left the area at the time of blood sample, leaving a total of 262 children with blood sample data at the end of the study."

Comment: Outcome data were analysed and available for a sub-sample (n=262) of 1000 children 6-30 months randomised.

Outcome data were analysed in a sub-sample of participants with no analysis methods or sensitivity analysis to ascertain the relationship between the sub-selected outcome data (analysed vs. not re-enroled) and its true value. 

Authors report only analysing outcome data in a sub-selected sample of randomised children; thus, missingness (including reasons for missingness) in the outcome data is unrelated the outcome.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "The blood specimen was centrifuged (Remi Sales & Engineering LtD, Mumbai, India) at approx. 450 x g at room temperature for 10 min in field settings. Plasma was separated and transferred into storage vials, and stored at -20°C at the central laboratory until analysis. HemoCue AB (HemoCue Hb Angelholm, Sweden) was used to analyze Hb concentration [15,16]. "

Comment: Hemocue with capillary blood vs. venous blood samples. However, laboratory method used in outcome assessment conforms to a valid and appropriate method. The use of a standardised laboratory method in outcome assessment likely ensures comparable methods across treatment groups and time points. In clinical trials registration, masking was quadruple (participant, care provider, investigator and outcome assesor). There is indication from the trials registry that outcome assessors were unaware of treatment group assignments.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement:
Quote: "This manuscript reports on the effect of the interventions on the Hb concentration and iron status at end of study which were predefined secondary outcomes of this study."

"In the table of baseline data, continuous variables were reported as means or medians as appropriate and categorical variables as proportions. We log transformed the plasma folate, vitamin B-12, and tHcy concentrations. The mean differences and the corresponding 95% CIs were compared by using t tests, and differences between the groups are expressed as geometric mean ratios."

"Continuous variables are given as means (SD), or medians (interquartile range) or means of log transformed values (SD)."

"We investigated the effect of folic acid and vitamin B12 supplementation
given for 6 months on the concentration of hemoglobin and other biomarkers in multiple regression analyses."

Comment: Recruitment for the trial was from January 2010 to September 2011. Trial (NCT00717730) was registered on 2008-07-16. Although the outcome is not specified in the trials registry, there is indication from the published report that outcome data conforms to a pre-specified analysis plan. Outcome results are reported as pre-specified in the trials registry at baseline and at the end of the study (6 months).

Based on the statistical analysis plan, numerical results were reported accordingly as means (SD) at baseline and at the end of the study for all treatment groups. There is no indication that outcome results are selected from multiple eligible analysis.
